title: 'Cruel abuser enjoyed' terrorising partner
description: He subjected his partner to a campaign of violence and "psychological manipulation", a court hears.
fullText:
A "cruel" domestic abuser who got "enjoyment" out of terrorising his partner has been jailed for two and a half years.

Daniel Kane's campaign of violence and "psychological manipulation" against the woman included headbutting her, abandoning her at a service station and destroying her phone in a microwave, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

The woman said she had felt "powerless" and in constant fear of what Kane would do next during the almost two-year long relationship.

Kane, 47, and from Woolsington, Newcastle, admitted offences including coercive and controlling behaviour, with his barrister saying he was "riddled" with an alcohol addiction at the time.

Kane and the woman began a relationship in July 2021 but as he began to drink more heavily his behaviour towards her deteriorated, prosecutor Nick Lane said.

He would "lash out at her for no reason", with the first violence four months into the relationship seeing him drag her round by her hair, the court heard.

When the woman later challenged him about the attack, he said he had "done that to prove a point" and he could "act on anyway he wanted", Lane said.

In November 2022, the couple stopped at a service station on their way back from Manchester, with Kane becoming angry when the pair got separated in the building, the court heard.

He took her mobile phone and drove off, returning a short while later and telling her it had been "funny" to see the look on her face and how upset she had been, the court heard.

Kane would frequently march her out of their home by her neck, told her what to wear and threatened to rip her finger nails off if he did not like how they had been styled, Lane said.

He was verbally abusive and "deliberately" called the woman by the name of his previous partner knowing it upset her, the court heard.

When she said she wanted to leave, Kane would threaten to harm himself, the court was told, with the woman saying that "pressure" and "psychological manipulation" was the reason she stayed with him.

In December 2022, he destroyed her phone in a microwave, then punched her in the face before telling her it was her fault and asking if she had "learned her lesson", the court heard.

The following February, he headbutted and punched her in the face following a row over a misplaced TV remote control, Lane said.

The woman would tell relatives her injuries were caused in accidents, with Kane sitting and "smirking" beside her as she lied to cover for him, the court heard.

In May 2023, the woman finally ended the relationship, prompting Kane to bombard her with abusive phone calls and voicemails, in one of which he demanded she give him £10,000 or he would shoot her and her family, the court heard.

Lane said the abuse was "cruel", adding Kane had "manipulated" the woman and seemed to have obtained "enjoyment" from behaving the way he did towards her.

In a statement read to the court, the woman said the "degrading, painful and terrifying" abuse had been "ongoing" and made her feel "powerless, frightened and controlled".

She said she was often in physical pain and felt "completely helpless" and in fear of "what he might do next".

The woman said she still had frequent nightmares about Kane and had become "extremely paranoid".

In mitigation, Rachel Hedworth said a now-sober Kane was "sickened to his core" by his actions, with the abuse occurring while he was "so riddled and addled" by an alcohol addiction.

"He has so little recollection of what went on and has found it very difficult to come to terms with this monster-like behaviour," she said, adding he had done "everything humanly possible to try to rehabilitate himself" in the three years since the relationship ended.

The court heard the case had taken two years to conclude in the courts, with Kane having only entered guilty pleas in July when his trial was due to start.

Recorder Jamie Hill KC said it was to Kane's "credit" he had "sought help" with addiction and mental health issues during the time the case was "strung out".

But while the abuser had moved his "life to a better place", the victim had "had to live not knowing" if she would need to go through the trauma of reliving her experiences at a trial.

The impact of the abuse had been "enormous" and continued to affect the woman's life, the judge said, adding: "She clearly bears the mental scars of what you did to her.

"She continues to live with the trauma."

A restraining order banning Kane from contacting the woman was made to last indefinitely.

title: I tried Burger King's revamped chicken nuggets. They're a much-needed upgrade.
description: I tried the new chicken nuggets from Burger King, part of the chain's mission to update some of its core menu items. They were an improvement.
fullText:
Burger King has finally given its chicken nuggets an upgrade.

The chain overhauled its nuggets after customers complained they were "dry" and "rubbery."

I thought the new, crispier chicken nuggets were a great value compared to others on the market.

After customers branded Burger King's chicken nuggets "dry," "rubbery," and "disappointing," the chain decided enough was enough — and gave its smallest chicken offering a big makeover.

Released September 1, the new chicken nuggets are crispier than the original nuggets, which were first added to menus in 1985. The recipe has also been updated to include a more flavorful marinade and new packaging, Burger King said.

It follows the chain's update to its signature Whopper in February with new box packaging, a new bun, and new "creamier" mayonnaise, in response to customer complaints that the burger — which used to be wrapped in paper — was often squished during transit.

In an August earnings call, the company said the updates to the Whopper were paying off. The chain reported that US same-store sales jumped 8.5% year over year in the second quarter, and customers bought about 20% more Whoppers than in the previous period.

When I spoke with leadership at Burger King headquarters in Miami in April, chief marketing officer Joel Yashinsky said the chain wasn't focused solely on menu innovation but also on upgrading its existing menu.

"We've been really working the last four years to improve the restaurant experience — our operations, our technology in the restaurants, remodeling — and we're also elevating our food," he said.

I tried Burger King's new chicken nuggets to see how they stack up against the original version.

The first thing I noticed when I ordered the nuggets was that they now came in a cardboard clamshell box.

Burger King made a similar update when it revamped the Whopper, but I was still surprised to see the chain introduce new packaging for its nuggets.

Burger King previously served its nuggets in paper bags, but I found the new box kept them much warmer during transit.

A 10-piece chicken nugget costs $5.19, excluding tax and fees, at my local Burger King in Brooklyn, New York.

I thought that was a good deal, considering that the same number of nuggets at McDonald's is $5.79, excluding tax and fees.

Right away, the nuggets looked crispier than the original version.

The nuggets had a deep golden color and a crisp, batter-like coating that reminded me more of McDonald's chicken nuggets than Burger King's original version.

Rather than the breadcrumb-heavy exterior of BK's classic nuggets, this breading was smoother with a slightly puffed texture that gave each piece a more uniform look.

The chicken nuggets also looked a little bigger than before and were more unevenly shaped.

There were small crumbs of fried breading across the nuggets' surfaces, adding texture to every bite.

I liked how the chicken nuggets paired with the chain's dipping sauces.

I particularly liked the nuggets with the chain's Zesty sauce, my go-to dip at Burger King.

The sauce's creamy, tangy flavor and slight kick of spice cut through the richness of the fried breading without overpowering the chicken.

Inside, there wasn't an overwhelming amount of chicken, but the nuggets were moist.

While there wasn't as much chicken inside as in some other fast-food nuggets, it was moist and savory with a slight sweetness, while the breading had a peppery taste.

Overall, I thought they were an excellent value for the price and, rather than feeling like a side to one of Burger King's burgers, the nuggets could now hold their own as a meal.

I preferred the new chicken nuggets to the original.

Unlike Burger King's old nuggets, which I found a little too heavily breaded to stand on their own, the new version felt more balanced and satisfying.

When I tried the original nuggets — which cost $3.89, excluding tax, for an eight-piece — I thought they worked better as an accompaniment to one of the chain's burgers, but I felt the new nuggets could serve as a meal.

I loved how the new version paired with the Zesty sauce, and the smoother, crispier coating let the flavor of the chicken come through more clearly than in the original.

Burger King's strategy of upgrading its existing menu worked for the Whopper, and I could see it proving just as successful for the fast-food giant's chicken lineup.

title: Federal appeals court upholds ban on Trump's bid to use citizenship data for voter checks
description: Sept 5 (Reuters) - A federal appeals court panel rejected the Trump administration’s bid to lift a ban on using a federal immigration database to check the accuracy of citizenship records on states' ‌
fullText:
Sept 5 (Reuters) - A federal appeals court panel rejected the Trump administration's bid to lift a ban on ‌using a federal immigration database to check the accuracy ‌of citizenship records on states' voter rolls.

In a 2-1 ruling on Friday, ​the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia declined to lift a lower court's ban on using the Homeland Security Department's Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements database. The earlier ruling ‌determined that the government ⁠cannot use the system ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which Trump's Republicans ⁠will be defending narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Chief Judge Sri Srinivasan and U.S. Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, both appointed ​to the ​appeals court by President Barack ​Obama, upheld the lower ‌court decision that the SAVE system violates the Social Security Act as it shares millions of Americans' private information. The appeals court judges also noted concerns around the potential for inaccurate citizen information that could lead to people having to prove ‌citizenship to remain registered voters, and ​in some cases could even lead ​to voter registration being ​canceled.

U.S. Circuit Judge Gregory Katsas, an appointee ‌of President Donald Trump, dissented.

A federal ​judge in ​Florida in July ordered the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to resume giving four Republican-led states access to the ​database after another ‌judge blocked it from continuing to use the ​database nationwide.

title: Judge rules former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema can now be sued under NC ‘homewrecker’ law
description: A federal judge ruled Friday that former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema (I-Ariz.) can be sued under North Carolina’s homewrecker law for her romantic relationship with a married member of her security detail. Si...
fullText:
A federal judge ruled Friday that former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema (I-Ariz.) can be sued under North Carolina's homewrecker law for her romantic relationship with a married member of her security detail.

Sinema has admitted to having a relationship with Matthew Ammel in 2024, but her attorneys have argued she cannot be sued in North Carolina because she has no ties to the state.

U.S. District Judge David A. Bragdon denied the former lawmaker's request to dismiss a lawsuit brought by the security guard's ex-wife, Heather Ammel.

Sinema sent nine text messages to Matthew Ammel while he was at his North Carolina home, which Bragdon determined gives the state jurisdiction over the case.

"These messages, considered together, show Ms. Sinema building and furthering a romantic relationship with Mr. Ammel—invading the marriage not just while he was away on trips with her but while he was home with his family in North Carolina," the judge wrote in his order.

North Carolina is one of the select states where people can sue for "alienation of affection," which allows spouses to seek damages from the person responsible for breaking up their marriage.

Heather Ammel sued the former senator at the end of last year, seeking at least $75,000 from Sinema.

The former Sinema security guard's ex-wife alleged she had "a good and loving marriage" prior to the former lawmaker's interference. The couple separated on Nov. 1, 2024.

She argued Sinema's messages to her then-husband "exceeded the bounds of a normal working relationship and were of romantic and lascivious natures."

The lawsuit also claimed the former lawmaker paid for Matthew Ammel's psychedelic treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder, substance abuse and traumatic brain injuries resulting from his military deployments.

title: I resigned and couldn't find a job. I lived with family, lost my storage unit, and relied on government assistance.
description: Kymberly McClain struggled to find work after resigning from her nonprofit role. She shared how she navigated her nearly two-year job search.
fullText:
Kymberly McClain struggled to find work for nearly two years after resigning from her nonprofit role.

She eventually deleted her LinkedIn account out of frustration and relied on government assistance.

McClain shared how she navigated her long job search and eventually found a call center job.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kymberly McClain, a 45-year-old who lives in Las Vegas. She previously worked at a small nonprofit until resigning in 2024. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

Two years ago, I was working as a deputy director at a small nonprofit in California focused on providing resources for the homeless population.

After some leadership changes, I didn't feel like I had the support I needed. In August 2024, I resigned.

When I started looking for a new job, I was so confident. I'd gained experience and felt like I'd parted ways on good terms, even getting a letter of recommendation.

I thought I was going to slide into another role. Instead, I struggled to find work for nearly two years.

When I started looking, I was applying for deputy director, program manager, case manager, and other social service roles.

I used LinkedIn, Indeed, ZipRecruiter, CareerBuilder, and other job sites. I sought out résumé help because I had been out of the job market for a few years and didn't know what had changed.

September, October, November, and December went by, and nothing happened.

As the search continued, I started broadening the scope of the types of jobs I was applying for. I went from thinking I could easily land another deputy director job to applying for retail jobs at places like Burlington Coat Factory. I was willing to take anything.

Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form, emailing him, or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here.

LinkedIn was probably the platform I used most during the first six months of my search.

I went to LinkedIn training sessions about how to get a job and read up on interview tips. At one point, I was applying to multiple jobs a day and changing my résumé for each one. I would research the company and position before applying.

But I wasn't having any luck. I remember seeing comments from other people on LinkedIn asking whether anyone else was having trouble finding a job or getting employers to respond.

As the rejections piled up, I started questioning everything. Was it my race? My age? My lack of a college education? I even wondered whether I was on somebody's list of people not to hire. I had never imagined that I would be without a job for this long.

After about a year of searching, I was exhausted by the rejection. I started pulling back from my job search and eventually deleted my LinkedIn account out of frustration. I thought, What's the point?

My job search took a toll on my finances, and I had to apply for government assistance. For a while, I went back and forth between staying with a friend in California and with family in Las Vegas while I tried to figure things out. Eventually, I moved in with my family members in Las Vegas.

Eventually, I felt like I needed to contribute financially to the household. I had to choose between helping my family and paying for the storage unit I'd stored my belongings in when I moved, so I gave up the unit and lost the belongings in it.

When I wasn't looking for work, I focused more of my time on a nonprofit I'd founded years earlier, based partly on my own experiences navigating the social services system. It helps people experiencing homelessness and domestic violence survivors navigate housing and other resources.

It wasn't generating income, but I needed to feel like I was doing something productive.

Earlier this year, I gave the job market another try. I applied for several healthcare billing roles, but I was rejected from all of them.

Then, my daughter sent me a link to a remote customer-service job. I completed an assessment, went through the process, and got a yes.

It's a full-time customer-service call center job. It pays significantly less than I made in my prior role, but after being out of work for so long, I'm just excited somebody said yes. When I got the offer, I thought, Okay, I'm not blackballed from the job market.

I'm still not sure what the future holds, but I plan to keep working on my nonprofit while I work this new job.

My advice to other job seekers is to have faith in closed doors. Sometimes rejection is redirection, and sometimes it's the push you need to build something of your own.

title: The Venezuelan billionaire the US investigated for money laundering now has a Pentagon oil deal
description: , Marianna Parraga and Gram Slattery CARACAS/MIAMI, Sept 5 (Reuters) - The billionaire who helped broker the Trump administration’s sweeping long-term oil deal with Venezuela was
fullText:
CARACAS/MIAMI, Sept 5 (Reuters) - The billionaire who helped broker the Trump administration's sweeping long-term oil deal with Venezuela was until recently a target of U.S. money-laundering investigations involving funds embezzled from the state-owned oil company PDVSA. Now, after assisting U.S. authorities ahead of the capture of authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro, Alejandro Betancourt is Washington's key partner in an unusual oil agreement with Caracas.

According to last week's announcement, the U.S. gains access to about one-fifth of Venezuela's crude reserves for decades. The Pentagon's ‌Office of Strategic Capital takes a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), Betancourt's company and a known crude producer in Venezuela. The State Department gets the right to buy 20% of NABEP's oil at cost, and preferential access to the remaining 80% of output.

The deal marks ‌a striking change of fortune for Betancourt, who four people familiar with U.S. policy in Venezuela said was key to U.S. strategy and planning in the lead-up to the January 3 operation that removed former President Maduro from power and flew him to New York to face charges of drug-trafficking, which Maduro denies.

Asked about the investigations of Betancourt, a U.S. official who declined to be named ​said most of the legal challenges were nearly a decade old — and that he currently has no legal problems in the United States. NABEP's record of pumping oil in Venezuela made Betancourt the best partner to help boost output under the arrangement, the official said.

Sarah Chouraqui, NABEP's lawyer, said Betancourt had a strong record of operating in complex energy markets. "The allegations in question have been examined extensively by authorities in multiple jurisdictions, and no charges have been brought against him," she said in an email.

Chouraqui did not address questions about his assistance to the Trump administration or his legal cases.

INFORMATION THAT HELPED ENFORCE U.S. BLOCKADE

In the months before Maduro's capture, the billionaire provided information that helped enforce a U.S. naval blockade targeting sanctioned oil tankers operating in Venezuela, which led to the seizure or interdiction of more than a dozen vessels, according to the four people who spoke on ‌condition of anonymity. He also facilitated negotiations with officials including Delcy Rodriguez, who became interim president after Maduro's capture.

The ⁠Venezuelan government did not respond to requests for comment.

After Maduro's removal, Betancourt's role as a key intermediary continued, helping broker oil deals and other partnerships and continuing to assist communications between Washington and Caracas to kickstart Venezuela's economy, according to seven sources.

In January, Betancourt helped broker a key oil trading agreement that has led to the export of more than 135 million barrels of crude and fuel to the United States, Europe, India and the Caribbean so far, according to vessel monitoring data and ⁠six people with knowledge of the negotiations. That's about half of all oil exports through the end of August.

Betancourt has also popped in on meetings at Venezuela's Miraflores presidential palace, according to two people familiar with the matter. He was also at Miraflores during this week's visit by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Wright told reporters, though Betancourt did not appear with Wright and Rodriguez at a signing ceremony for oil deals.

Betancourt has been investigated in the United States, Spain and Switzerland but never indicted.

Earlier this year U.S. federal prosecutors in Florida paused their investigation into Betancourt in connection with an alleged plan that involved embezzling over $1 billion from Venezuela's state-owned oil company ​and ​laundering it through real estate in Miami and bank accounts in Malta and Switzerland.

Two of those people said U.S. prosecutors had been subsequently discouraged by supervisors from investigating Betancourt further.

Prosecutors ​on the case were not given a rationale, four people familiar with the case said.

After the investigation stalled, U.S. officials ‌pressured the Swiss government to ease its inquiries into the tycoon, said four people familiar with the matter. Switzerland, which was also investigating Betancourt for money-laundering, dropped its request to extradite him from the United Kingdom in May, said the sources.

The Zurich Public Prosecutor's Office declined to comment on whether the United States influenced the decision to withdraw its extradition request, but said the case against Betancourt was still proceeding.

"The extradition request was withdrawn because of particular aspects of UK extradition law, which we cannot discuss in detail," the Office said. "This step concerns only the extradition proceedings in the UK. The criminal proceedings against the accused are otherwise unaffected and will continue."

The withdrawal was unusual, said Mark Pieth, a Swiss legal scholar and anti-corruption expert. "You would not do that if the case is continuing," he said.

The United Kingdom's Home Office declined to comment.

A YOUNG GENERATION OF BUSINESS LEADERS

Betancourt is a prominent member of the so-called Bolichicos — a younger generation of business people who amassed fortunes during the administration of former Venezuelan leader Hugo Chavez. His company Derwick Associates won roughly $2 billion in government contracts to build power plants during the country's electricity crisis in the 2010s — some without competitive bidding — despite having little construction experience.

Government data later showed many of the plants operated at a fraction of their intended capacity or not ‌at all, as Venezuela's power grid continued to suffer widespread blackouts. Betancourt and Derwick have repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said the facilities were completed and that later failures resulted from ​mismanagement by state authorities. Rodriguez told a press conference on Wednesday that all legal proceedings against Betancourt's companies in Venezuela were dismissed years ago.

In 2012, Betancourt entered into a partnership with state-controlled ​company PDVSA to operate mature fields in western Venezuela. These would eventually become the core production of NABEP, which Betancourt co-founded with Florida billionaire Harry ​Sargeant in April 2024. Sargeant sold his shares in NABEP last month.

Mauricio Claver-Carone, a Miami businessman and former Trump administration adviser who implemented U.S. policy in Caracas in an unofficial role, told Reuters last month that Betancourt is a useful intermediary between the ‌Trump administration and Rodriguez because he understands the oil business in both countries. He added that Betancourt had been ​helpful to the first Trump administration.

But several former U.S. intelligence officials, prosecutors and diplomats ​privately expressed concern regarding Betancourt's influence on U.S. policy, because of the previous investigation in the U.S. and ongoing investigation in Switzerland, as well as his proximity to high-ranking officials from the former Hugo Chavez and Maduro governments.

Federal prosecutors are "scratching their heads," said one former prosecutor with knowledge of the situation.

Before the Miami-based investigation into Betancourt was put on hold, six sources said he had been identified as an unnamed unindicted co-conspirator in an alleged plan by former Venezuelan energy officials and their associates to launder more than $1 billion misappropriated from the state-owned PDVSA oil company. Ten people have ​been indicted since 2018.

In Spain, authorities launched a new investigation into Betancourt for money laundering last year involving $4 billion ‌allegedly embezzled from PDVSA, according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.

Spain's National Court and the Venezuelan state oil company did not respond to requests for comment.

Once he was free to leave the UK, Betancourt traveled to Venezuela in ​late June and again in July, both times departing from West Palm Beach, Florida, according to flight manifests seen by Reuters.

Betancourt's lawyer Chouraqui did not comment on his travel.

title: US strikes 3 Iranian oil tankers after saying warships were targeted with ballistic missiles
description: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy warships were targeted with ballistic missiles, the American military said Saturday, warning that it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited...
fullText:
CAIRO (AP) — U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy warships were targeted with ballistic missiles, the American military said Saturday, warning that it would "if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet." Experts called it a dangerous escalation after Iran's previous attacks at sea targeted commercial shipping.

The strikes — a day after U.S. President Donald Trump sought to minimize the conflict as "small potatoes" — keep up a new tilt back toward fighting after six months of on-again, off-again war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on the country on Feb. 28. Both sides have sought to inflict both military and economic pain, and negotiations have collapsed.

The military's statement said an American aircraft carrier and a destroyer evaded "multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks" while patrolling in the region and no U.S. personnel were hurt. It wasn't clear when the Iranian missiles were fired. The statement said that two Iranian oil carriers were "permanently disabled" and the third, unladen one, was destroyed.

The U.S. statement called the tankers part of a shadow network helping to fund Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies in the region.

A spokesperson with Iran's joint military command later warned that strikes against U.S. military ships would be more severe, if the U.S. continues to interfere with Iranian shipping, the state broadcaster reported.

That Iran targeted a U.S. aircraft carrier with a ballistic missile "indicates that Tehran is becoming increasingly willing to accept risks it previously sought to avoid, including directly threatening some of the most important U.S. military assets in the region," Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said on X.

Earlier, Iranian state television had said that four U.S. missiles struck a tanker about 6 miles (10 kilometers) from Kharg Island, home to a terminal through which the country exports most of its oil. Kharg Island has been repeatedly targeted during the war, including in U.S. strikes on military sites there in March.

The U.S. said that one tanker was struck off Kharg Island and another was struck near Jask, east of the Strait of Hormuz. The unladen tanker was hit in the Gulf of Oman, and the U.S. said its crew had been "directed to abandon ship." The statement shared what it called video footage of the strikes.

After the U.S. statement, Iran's state broadcaster reported the attack of the two other tankers, saying their crews had evacuated.

"We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet," said Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command.

Iran's Foreign Ministry called the attacks a war crime, and said that the consequences for continued U.S. aggression, including "economic warfare," would rest with Washington and its allies.

Between the war and the disabling of ships during the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, it's not immediately clear how many Iranian oil tankers have been targeted. On May 8, the U.S. military said that it fired "precision munitions" into the smokestacks of two Iranian oil tankers, both unladen.

The latest strikes came nearly a week after the U.S. and Iran resumed attacks following a month of relative calm, with the Strait of Hormuz, and Iranian communities along it again, being targeted. At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a U.S. bombardment of southern Iran. One strike hit a wedding.

Masoumeh Zarei, 13, was wounded in the attack. She spoke to The Associated Press at a hospital while being treated for injuries to her abdomen.

She said the wedding celebration had already begun when she set out to join it. She never made it there. She was knocked unconscious when a telecommunications tower was struck. Her next memory was of waking up in a hospital.

"The party had just started, and we wanted to go there," Zarei said, her voice hoarse. "I had made my nails really pretty for the party, but everything changed."

Her friend, 14-year-old Kiana Karimi, also was wounded and in intensive care. She told the AP that she heard five explosions.

"The first three explosions at the telecommunications tower threw us to the ground," Karimi said. "I quickly got up to pick my brothers up off the ground. Then there were two more explosions, and after that I don't remember anything."

The Trump administration appears to have adopted a dual-prong approach to the conflict, responding militarily to attacks on the strait while going after foreign financial institutions that handle Iran's money. U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Thursday said that there was no prospect for renewed talks as long as Iran goes after ships, while noting that major military operations ended in July.

But Tehran's hard-line new senior leaders have signaled the willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions. The elected government of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, however, has said that it favors a negotiated end to the war.

Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions — and now the U.S. blockade — and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil.

Meanwhile, the issue that helped lead to the war — Iran's nuclear program — was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June. Now diplomats say the U.S., Britain, France and Germany seek to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations.

Instead, Tehran's new leverage focuses on the strait that is crucial to global oil and natural gas shipments and was seen as an international waterway before the war began.

The U.S. military has been helping to guide ships through the strait as Tehran asserts control and targets some vessels, but overall traffic remains low.

Amir Vahdat reported from Minab, Iran. Cara Anna reported from Jerusalem. Matthew Lee contributed to this report from Washington.

title: Colorado man who was free on bond in wife's alleged killing is jailed after hit-and-run
description: A man in Colorado who had been free on $3 million bond in his wife's alleged killing was arrested Friday after prosecutors said he got in a hit-and-run crash with two other vehicles in Denver.  Barry ...
fullText:
BOULDER, Colo. (AP) — A man in Colorado who had been free on $3 million bond in his wife's alleged killing was arrested Friday after prosecutors said he got in a hit-and-run crash with two other vehicles in Denver.

Barry Morphew was booked into the Boulder County Jail. Alamosa County District Judge Amanda Hopkins set a hearing to discuss Morphew's bond Tuesday, online records show.

Under the terms of his bond set last year, Morphew was not supposed to travel away from home in southern Colorado except for work and other limited circumstances.

He got into the crash involving two other vehicles during a trip to Denver International Airport on Aug. 28, possibly to pick up his daughter, prosecutors said in a court filing.

"To go to the airport for any purpose other than work constitutes a breach of his bond," read the filing by District Attorney Anne Kelly.

Morphew's attorneys didn't immediately respond to phone and email messages seeking comment Friday.

Morphew has pleaded not guilty and faces trial next summer in the death of his wife, who disappeared in 2020.

Suzanne Morphew's skeletal remains were found off a dirt road in southern Colorado in 2023. By then, charges against Barry Morphew had been dropped, but he was charged again with first-degree murder in his wife's death and arrested.

Investigators found no sign of trauma in Suzanne Morphew's remains but allegedly found traces in her bone marrow of a drug cocktail used to tranquilize wildlife. Barry Morphew was the only person in the area other than wildlife officials with authorization to use the chemicals, prosecutors allege.

title: China rare earth firms halt some US shipments over geopolitical worries, sources say
description: , Solomon Cefai, Trevor Hunnicutt and Lewis Jackson BEIJING/SINGAPORE/WASHINGTON, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Some Chinese rare earth suppliers are declining to ship to the U.S. for fear of
fullText:
BEIJING/SINGAPORE/WASHINGTON, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Some Chinese rare earth suppliers are declining to ship to the U.S. for fear of repercussions from Beijing, three sources said, underscoring how access to the materials remains an issue for the U.S. weeks before President Xi Jinping visits Washington.

U.S. officials have repeatedly asked China to stick ‌to commitments made in Busan and Beijing over the past year to ensure the smooth flow of rare earth export licences. The persistence of the problem has put it on the U.S. ‌planning agenda ahead of Xi's September 24 visit, a source familiar with the work said.

A handful of Chinese suppliers have refused to ship rare earths to U.S. companies since early August when China imposed sanctions on the Responsible Business Alliance (RBA), a U.S. supply chain monitor, ​a separate source with direct knowledge of the situation said.

With China deploying its own trade compliance weapons, the companies were wary of punishment from Beijing for complying with the due diligence framework of the Responsible Minerals Initiative (RMI), a global mineral supply chain audit programme connected with the RBA, the source said.

Other Chinese rare earths companies had already stopped shipments to the U.S. to avoid entanglement in geopolitics in recent months, two other sources familiar with the trade said. One cited four instances where Chinese firms declined to send material for fear it could be resold to banned users.

The sources declined to be named given the issue's sensitivity.

A U.S. ⁠official speaking on condition of anonymity told Reuters that the administration continues to press Chinese counterparts to address China's lack of compliance with the Busan agreement, as well as other bilateral concerns.

While exports of many rare earths or related magnets have rebounded since China imposed restrictions in April 2025, the prices of certain rare earths and ⁠critical materials like yttrium, indium phosphide and tungsten that have military applications or are used in sensitive industries including aerospace or chipmaking remain near record highs with tight supply.

Other industries affected by licence delays include medical devices and energy.

Exports to the U.S. of yttrium have risen this year but are still only about half 2024 levels despite large shipments to other countries, Chinese customs data shows. Some U.S. companies have been waiting more than six months for mineral licences, said two ​of ​the sources, declining to identify them.

title: Judge reinforces order halting immediate work on Trump’s 250-foot arch
description: A judge ordered the Trump administration to provide 48 hours’ notice before construction begins on the site of President Donald Trump’s planned arch.
fullText:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Friday, Sept. 4, to provide 48 hours' notice before moving forward with work on the site of a planned 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that the administration must inform the court "before engaging in any activity on Memorial Circle other than on-site information gathering" to identify underground cultural artifacts.

Chutkan reinforced her order a day after Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum announced plans on Sept. 3 to break ground at the site of the arch in the coming days.

"We are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck, at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery," Burgum wrote on X. "This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World."

The proposed arch, one of several projects Trump has launched in an effort to change the landscape of the nation's capital, has been controversial from the start. A group of three veterans and a historian filed a lawsuit in February to oppose the project.

The plaintiffs asked Chutkan on Sept. 4 to issue a 14-day restraining order to block the Trump administration from "taking any steps to construct or to direct or facilitate construction of any structure in Memorial Circle."

Despite Burgum's announcement, the government argued in a court filing that the planned activity at the site of the proposed arch is standard archaeological survey work. The administration intends to mechanically excavate four test pits no earlier than Sept. 21 and the land is expected to be restored by Oct. 31, per the filing.

"This activity is not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch," the government said.

The proposed arch is also awaiting final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, which would need to grant an exception to a 130-foot building height limit.

title: Trump’s ‘Catch-Me-If-You-Can’ presidency keeps finding ways around the law
description: A plain reading of the law about presidents on coins says the face of a living president should not be on currency. And yet President Donald Trump’s is, after his Treasury Department exploited a diffe...
fullText:
A plain reading of the law about presidents on coins says the face of a living president should not be on currency. And yet President Donald Trump's is, after his Treasury Department exploited a different law related to commemorative coins.

The law says a president must not commit the US military into hostilities for longer than 60 days without congressional approval. The US has been in a conflict with Iran for more than six months, although the administration says it has taken time-outs in the war. Previous presidents from both parties have danced around this requirement, but nothing on the level of Trump's war on Iran.

Chief Justice John Roberts called it "likely unlawful" for Trump to tear down part of the White House and build something else. And yet construction is happening around the clock to get that White House ballroom done for Trump to enjoy.

Laws would seem to require Congress to approve the construction of a triumphal arch adjacent to Arlington National Cemetery. The administration isn't waiting and the Department of Interior appears primed to start excavation shortly.

The law says suspected criminals should not be put to death without a trial. And yet the US military has taken out numerous alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific.

The law says Congress creates agencies of the federal government, like USAID, the US Department of Education and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Trump has tried to end some of them anyway, either through starvation or outright deletion.

The law says Congress decides where money should go. That didn't stop Trump's administration from cutting research funding and aid money it simply disagreed with.

The law says the government should not be entering people's homes without a judicial warrant. But Immigration and Customs Enforcement has utilized that power.

The law says the Federal Reserve should operate independently, but that isn't stopping Trump from trying to pressure the Fed to lower interest rates — most recently via a threat to cease trade with top partners.

The list goes on, and with it the complicated legal arguments the Trump administration has made – in those instances when it has had to make them.

Even when faced with setbacks in court, Trump's administration has brazenly looked for end-runs.

A judge ruled Trump's administration can't ignore the law and put his name alongside John F. Kennedy's on the Kennedy Center. But the administration plans to add it to the building anyway, by adding an inscription giving Trump credit for the rehab job. And if the administration can't put the name on the building, it threatens to tear the whole thing down.

The tearing-down of buildings the president should not be able to tear down is an apt analogy for this whole presidency. Once something is gone, it's gone. It doesn't matter if getting rid of it was illegal.

Roberts sided with liberals on the court to argue – in an unsuccessful dissent – that Trump's East Wing project should be halted because it was "likely unlawful." In his dissent, Roberts quoted Winston Churchill during World War II.

"We shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us," Churchill had said. Roberts didn't mention that Churchill made those comments to argue the British House of Commons should be rebuilt as it had stood before it was destroyed by Nazi bombs. Churchill wanted to rebuild it as a monument to the British form of government.

Trump saw the White House East Wing as a tear-down project — a (likely) illegal tear-down in Roberts' eyes. But Trump's monument to himself – one of many — is getting built nonetheless. Asking Congress for the taxpayer money to help with the project came only after the walls were torn down.

It has become a pattern during Trump's second term that the president does something; Congress shrugs; and the Supreme Court allows him to proceed, regardless of whether what he's doing is, strictly speaking, legal.

A week before Roberts' historical lament, the liberal Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson blasted the court's conservatives, including Roberts, for allowing Trump's executive order meant to cut down on mail-in voting to proceed, again on a technicality.

The White House has a "Catch-Me-If-You-Can approach," Jackson said.

In the case of disrupting mail-in ballots, Trump may ultimately get caught; the executive order still faces lawsuits and a new injunction that make it seem impossible to impose, at least for this election.

Trump also got caught on birthright citizenship, where justices rejected his attempt to set aside the Constitution's 14th Amendment. And on tariffs, they said no, he could not exploit national emergency laws to upend the economy.

He's still looking for ways around that decision.

But on so many other issues, Trump's administration has picked the laws it wants to follow, diverted funds here or there, and said little in public about what it's up to. Congress has shrugged. Courts have had trouble keeping up, and the Supreme Court has preferred to let Trump go about his business while things get sorted out.

That dynamic seems likely to change, at least somewhat, come next year if Democrats win control of either the House or the Senate. They will try to restrict funding for Trump's goals.

But it will be an interesting question for Democrats who want to replace Trump in the White House in 2029. Should they spend even more taxpayer money to tear down the East Wing behemoth he's building? They won't be able to go back and take the coins with his face out of circulation. They can't un-deport people who didn't get a hearing. And it will take time and effort, if the next president is so inclined, to rebuild the system of scientific and medical research funding the Trump administration cut back.

On so many of the things Trump has done, catching up may not even be an option.

title: New season, same flaw - Chelsea title hopes already under scrutiny
description: With 11 minutes remaining, Chelsea appeared to be cruising to victory in their WSL opener against Aston Villa. So how did they throw it away?
fullText:
With 11 minutes remaining, Chelsea appeared to be cruising to victory in their Women's Super League opener against Aston Villa.

Yet, after 57 touches in the opposition box, 23 shots inside the area, hitting the crossbar and having another goal disallowed for offside, somehow they drew 1-1.

The statistics are alarming given they did everything right to win, except score more.

It is an issue that has reared its head on several occasions during manager Sonia Bompastor's time in charge and is why many have tipped rivals Arsenal to win the title this season.

While England international Lauren James oozed quality and summer signing Katie McCabe had a strong WSL debut, Chelsea's lack of ruthlessness in front of goal could prove costly.

"We started really well. We wanted to start with energy and create opportunities but at this level, we need to be more clinical," McCabe, who joined Chelsea from Arsenal this summer, told BBC Sport.

"We're frustrated to drop points at home. We're not going to panic - it's the start of the season. We'll look to rectify next week.

"But we're disappointed. It's not Chelsea standards to drop points at home."

Late own goal earns Aston Villa point at Chelsea

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Chelsea attempted 34 shots in the game, their highest total in a WSL match since the start of last season.

James hit the ground running with a superb strike that flew into the roof of the net within 11 minutes and Chelsea fans expected the floodgates to open.

Villa barely laid a glove on their opponents and had only five touches in Chelsea's box.

But, against the run of play, Noelle Maritz's shot ricocheted off goalkeeper Hannah Hampton and bounced in off Chelsea defender Veerle Buurman late on.

Villa boss Natalia Arroyo threw her arms in the air and their supporters punctured the silence of disbelief that fell across Stamford Bridge.

"If you analyse the performance and the statistics, then you would say it's crazy that we didn't win. We created so many opportunities," said Bompastor.

"The reality of football is that if we were two or three nil up then the game is over. It's a completely different game in the second half.

"We have to speed up the game, keep that momentum and sustain that. We need to make sure we accelerate to kill the game. That is not what happened today.

"At the end, we are all frustrated because it's not a good result."

Bompastor's biggest frustration was that she could do little to help.

With summer signing Melvine Malard out with a minor injury picked up in training and Mayra Ramirez still continuing her recovery, attacking options were limited.

England forward Aggie Beever-Jones led the line, taking the baton from recently-departed Sam Kerr, but her confidence is clearly low.

She had opportunities but scuppered them and when she did eventually put the ball in the net, it was ruled out for offside.

"What can we do in this scenario? We have to stay confident, stick together and work hard," said manager Bompastor.

"In football some of these things are mental. It's the mentality - the mindset of being ruthless and clinical in the box.

"The best teams don't need many opportunities. They just need one or two and maybe that's enough to win the game. That is something we need to work on."

This was not the first time Chelsea have dropped points because of a lack of ruthlessness.

Despite beginning the 25-26 WSL campaign with victory over eventual champions Manchester City, they ended up finishing third.

Four draws proved costly, on top of three defeats - one particular loss at Everton in December ending a 585-day unbeaten streak in the WSL.

In that 1-0 defeat, Chelsea had 79% possession, 30 shots and hit the woodwork three times. It was deja vu against Aston Villa on Saturday.

"You should be able to convert those chances. In the first half, they had chance after chance," said former England striker Ellen White on BBC One.

"To go for the title you have to score and get points on the board. This is two points dropped. Last season, they only dropped six points at home."

Manchester City begin their title defence on Sunday at home to newly-promoted Birmingham City (14:30 BST), while Arsenal travel to Brighton (12:00 BST).

That will give Chelsea a better idea of their competition after London City Lionesses put down a marker with a win at home to Manchester United on Friday night.

Bompastor hopes the return of other attacking players will improve their conversion rate going forward.

But the biggest issue is the hardest one to find a solution for at Chelsea.

"Some things are easier to coach and other things are more difficult. The mindset you can improve, but you have to have a killer instinct and desire inside," she added.

"We need to stay together and a lot of this is keeping the confidence. We just need to analyse all these things to help the players be confident for the next game."

title: University pays professor $600K after being punished for parodying land acknowledgments
description: Stuart Reges parodied the University of Washington's land acknowledgment on his syllabus, triggering censorship and a nearly yearlong investigation.
fullText:
The University of Washington has paid a professor $600,000 after punishing him for parodying a land acknowledgment in his syllabus.

Stuart Reges, a non-tenured computer science and engineering teaching professor at the university, said in his complaint that in September 2020, university officials encouraged professors (but did not require) to include the university's land acknowledgment statement in their class syllabus. Land acknowledgments are statements commonly used by universities and public institutions to recognize Native American tribes as the original inhabitants of the land on which campuses now sit.

Reges parodied the university's land acknowledgment in his Computer Programming II class syllabus in January 2022. Instead of using the university's land acknowledgment, he wrote, "I acknowledge that by the labor theory of property the Coast Salish people can claim historical ownership of almost none of the land currently occupied by the University of Washington."

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) said that Reges was punished for his actions.

"UW was not amused. University officials censored Reges' parody statement from his syllabus and created a competing class, so students could choose not to take a computer science class from Reges. The university also initiated a nearly year-long investigation of Reges under an 'antiharassment policy,'" the organization said.

Woke Stunt Goes Horribly Wrong As Michigan Dems Open Convention With Brutal 'Land Acknowledgment'

On Thursday, FIRE announced that Reges' legal battle had concluded with the settlement, following a Ninth Circuit ruling last December in his favor. Under the settlement, the university may take no further action against him over the parody statement.

Reges said in FIRE's press release, "I am deeply grateful to FIRE for this legal victory which will remind public universities that they are obligated to respect the First Amendment rights of their students, faculty, and staff."

He added, "More importantly, I hope that my protest can help reverse a decade-long trend towards ideological conformity in academia and help to convince them that instead of 'protecting' students from controversial ideas, they should be helping them to learn how to cope with disagreement. Only then can we heal the deep divisions that confront us today."

Gabe Walters, a FIRE attorney, told Fox News Digital:

"Professor Reges parodied UW's land acknowledgment statement knowing doing so might cause offense, but his deeper purpose was to encourage his colleagues to see beyond their partisan perspectives and consider that others might disagree with them. Epistemic humility is necessary to test ideas, and there's no better place to put ideas to the test than our colleges and universities," Walters said.

Controversial Streamer Hasan Piker's Lecture Axed By University Of Washington Amid Free Speech Questions

He added that the case could be better understood by looking at it from the angle of other hot-button issues.

"Consider the flip side of the coin: a state that bans professors from putting indigenous land acknowledgment statements in their syllabi also is putting its thumb improperly on the scale of public debate, and as a non-partisan organization dedicated to the freedom of speech and academic freedom, FIRE also would represent the hypothetical professor who wants to include a sincere land acknowledgment on their syllabi but is prohibited from doing so — just as we've challenged Florida's 'Stop WOKE Act' and Texas's campus ban on drag performances."

The University of Washington provided the following statement to Fox News Digital:

"The University of Washington maintains that we acted appropriately, and this settlement is in no way an admission of any wrongdoing. Given the Ninth Circuit's 2-1 decision overturning the federal district court's decision in favor of the University, a settlement agreement was the most reasonable option due to the attorney fees and costs that would have resulted from the Ninth's Circuit's decision. Prof. Reges has retained his faculty position and continued teaching throughout this process, and his status with the UW remains unchanged."

title: Ty Cobb on midterms: Trump intends ‘to steal these elections where possible’
description: Former Trump White House lawyer Ty Cobb said Thursday that President Trump would attempt to “steal” the 2026 midterm elections “where possible.” Cobb, in an appearance on MS NOW, discussed reports of ...
fullText:
Former Trump White House lawyer Ty Cobb said Thursday that President Trump would attempt to "steal" the 2026 midterm elections "where possible."

Cobb, in an appearance on MS NOW, discussed reports of GOP lawmakers declining to attend a Republican National Committee event, underlining concerns about Trump's political brand almost two years into his second term.

A source familiar told The Hill that the National Republican Congressional Committee distributed more than 2,000 tickets for the convention and that around 100 members and candidates were confirmed to attend. Lawmakers are expected to contribute a minimum of $25,000 to take part.

"Well, I think the Republicans who are saying no are being strategic," Cobb said. "But at the same time, he's [Trump] sitting on $400 million in campaign money that he could donate to some of these elections. And he's not."

Cobb added that, "It also plays into a narrative that I think people are undervaluing, which is I think Trump doesn't feel he needs to spend this money because it is his intention to interfere with the elections and to steal these elections where possible."

He raised the possibility that Trump could "urge" House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to refuse to swear in Democratic candidates following the midterm elections. Johnson was an active backer of Trump's efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss to former President Biden.

The Trump administration is still pushing to restrict mail-in voting for the midterms, even as states start sending out early ballots. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to allow for the U.S. Postal Service's implementation of Trump's executive order targeting mail voting.

The Postal Service's plan would mandate that states' mail-in ballots meet design requirements — such as unique barcodes and an official logo — and require election officials to upload lists of voters who are eligible to vote by mail. If a ballot doesn't meet the specifications or someone is not on the submitted list, the service would refuse to deliver it.

In a July appearance on MS NOW, Cobb argued that moves from Trump like this are rooted in his refusal to accept his 2020 defeat.

"The most grievous thing that ever happened to him was he lost an election," he said at the time. "As a malignant narcissist, he just can't abide that."

title: Fernandez and Ndiaye show signs of promise on Man City debuts
description: Manchester City gave £185m of deadline-day talent their Premier League debuts in the win over Coventry - and manager Enzo Maresca will have enjoyed what he saw.
fullText:
Manchester City gave £185m worth of talent signed on transfer deadline day their Premier League debuts in the 1-0 Premier League victory over Coventry and manager Enzo Maresca will have been quietly satisfied with what he saw from his new duo.

Midfielder Enzo Fernandez, brought in from Chelsea for £125m, was initially named as a substitute but was given a late call-up into the starting XI after Nico O'Reilly sustained a knock in the warm-up, while £60m Iliman Ndiaye also played from the off.

Both players have had limited time on the training ground with their new team-mates, but showcased early signs of what they will bring to the side and how competition for starting places has ramped up at Etihad Stadium.

Maresca knows Fernandez from his time in charge at Chelsea, with the pair winning the Europa Conference League and Club World Cup together, and he played a pivotal role in Erling Haaland's winning goal.

Maresca said: "It is much more easier when a player you already share time together [joins] because they know exactly what you want.

"We know each other very well, I know how good he is and I know that he is going to help the team to win games."

Man City maintain 100% start with win over Coventry

City clung on to a nervy victory against the Sky Blues to maintain their 100% winning start to the season, but managed to get the job done courtesy of a string of saves from goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Haaland continued his fine start to the season by converting his third goal in as many games from Antoine Semenyo's deep cross, which came after Fernandez played through a slide-rule pass to the Ghanaian.

Playing in the number eight role, Argentina international Fernandez was given licence to roam and make late bursts into the box - he touched the ball six times in the opposition area, with only Haaland managing more with 11.

Fernandez could have had a dream debut but saw two shots blocked, before being replaced after 76 minutes by fellow summer signing Ayyoub Bouaddi.

The 18-year-old Morocco international was part of City's midfield rebuild and highlights the options available to Maresca despite the departures of Bernardo Silva, Rodri, Tijjani Reijnders and Nico Gonzalez.

Ndiaye, meanwhile, became the first Senegalese player to represent City and is bound to give opposition defenders with his trickery and pace. No player attempted more dribbles in the match than his eight.

Maresca said: "Enzo and Iliman [played their] first game with us and then Ayyoub and Ryan [McAidoo] their first game in front of our fans.

"That is why I said there are many reasons I am happy about our win. I think they were all good.

"Ili just had two sessions with us. He needs to understand how to move. Most of the time he was moving in the wrong way, wrong position, but he needs to learn and for sure he is going to learn."

Asked to elaborate on Ndiaye's performance, Maresca said: "When Marc Guehi has the ball and he was dropping a lot and we don't need that.

"We need him in the last third so he can be a little bit more higher. That space was more for Josko Gvardiol.

"It is the same thing in this [other] side. But it is normal and with time they will learn the way we want them to play."

City's deadline-day deals make it easy to forget that England international Elliot Anderson also joined this summer for £116m from Nottingham Forest.

The 23-year-old is beginning to find his feet in a City shirt, being named man of the match against Coventry despite the travelling team threatening to cause a huge upset.

Frank Lampard's side could not take their chances and Anderson ended the game completing 143 of his 155 passes, four more than the Coventry team.

"Really impressed," said Maresca. "Not just today. He was very good against Palace; he was also very good against Bournemouth, having only been one week with us when we changed him for cramp.

"But the best thing with Elliot is the day by day. He is asking how he can learn. We sit with him one-v-one video [analysis] and he wants to be better, and that is the best thing for any player."

Former England international Lampard added: "He is a really good player. I admire him from afar and did at Forest, but this was the first time I had seen him close up in the flesh.

"Very smart, very talented and a very good player - good brain, everything you need in a midfield player - and he is going to be a fantastic player for Manchester City.

"He had a lot of the ball today. I don't think he could hurt us, but he was constantly on it and I highly respect players like that, no doubt."

title: Yen's changing fortunes might finally be spooking the bears
description: , Rae Wee and Atsuko Aoyama LONDON/SINGAPORE/TOKYO, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Six weeks after hitting a four-decade low against the dollar, the tide appears to be turning for the battered
fullText:
LONDON/SINGAPORE/TOKYO, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Six weeks after hitting a four-decade low against the dollar, the tide appears to be turning for the battered yen as a host of factors finally smoke out traders who have spent years betting against the Japanese currency.

While central bank rate hikes and record currency intervention have failed to provide lasting support for the ‌yen, new tailwinds from capital repatriation, unwinding carry trades and U.S. political pressure are now giving short speculators cause to rethink their long-term game.

The yen is on track for a roughly 2% surge against ‌the greenback this week — the most since a rare joint U.S. and Japan intervention at the end of July to lift the yen.

"The market psychology around the yen appears to be changing," said Rong Ren Goh, a fixed income portfolio manager at Eastspring Investments. "Investors seem increasingly reluctant to ​aggressively short the JPY (yen), particularly with the prospect of a BOJ rate hike in September adding another layer of risk to the trade."

The Bank of Japan is expected to lift its key rate by 25 basis points (bps) this month and markets are also contemplating the possibility of a 50-bps hike or a series of rapid increases in coming months.

Nevertheless, a 50-bps September hike is still seen as extremely unlikely, particularly under Governor Kazuo Ueda's cautious leadership.

All the same, the shift in mood is backed up by money flows. Data from Citigroup indicate positioning on the yen has flipped from bearish to bullish since the start of August, with interbank flow data showing leveraged funds, banks and real-money investors all net-buying yen this week.

The convergence ‌of central bank policy, investment flows and speculative positioning is adding to volatility. The ⁠yen is also up almost 2% against the euro and Australian dollar this week.

Stephen Jen, CEO and co-CIO of Eurizon SLJ Asset Management, said the risk of a rapid unwind of yen-based carry trades is rising, in a similar way to 1998 when the collapse of Long-Term Capital Management forced banks and hedge funds to rapidly deleverage.

The yen has long ⁠been the favoured currency for the carry trade, where investors borrow cheaply in yen to invest elsewhere.

"When a currency is so extremely undervalued, and positioning is so extended, movements like this one will occur increasingly frequently before a big move," Jen said. "It's a bit like earthquakes. The tectonic plates are grating on each other with great forces."

title: Ex-Fetterman staffers promise more damaging details after blistering report: ‘Tip of the iceberg’
description: Former staff members for John Fetterman launched an X account promising damaging revelations well beyond The Wall Street Journal report.
fullText:
In just over a week, former staffers for John Fetterman, D-Pa., are planning to go public with inside details after expressing what they called disgust at his work as a legislator.

"We're a group of former campaign & Senate staffers for John Fetterman who are disgusted with what he's become. If you were troubled by yesterday's Wall Street Journal story... trust us, that's just the tip of the iceberg," the group wrote in a post to X.

"It's even worse than you thought."

The new social media account, which is calling itself "Former Fetterman Staffers" (FFS) claims it will reveal additional unflattering details about the embattled senator's office as he also faces blowback over Wall Street Journal reporting chronicling his reluctance to engage in the basic duties of his office.

Fetterman Faces Dem Revolt As Bombshell Report Fuels Push To Oust Him: 'Disgrace'

The FFS acronym notoriously also stands for "for f---s sake."

Fetterman routinely blew off constituent meetings, neglected legislative review and declined to make in-state public appearances, according to a Wall Street Journal report published Thursday, drawing immediate backlash online.

"There is a lot I could say about this report of John Fetterman's pathetic behavior as a senator," Rep. Chris Deluzio, D-Pa., said on X. "But between the laziness, disrespect, and willingness to carry water for a foreign government, it shows us something we already know: this man has no sense of duty."

"John Fetterman is a disgrace," Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., said in a post of his own. "Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job."

Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta, who is the vice chair of the Democratic National Committee, also condemned Fetterman's behavior.

"This report is horrifying, but not new to many of us in PA. John barely showed up as [Lieutenant Governor] and is constantly MIA as our senator," Kenyatta wrote.

"When he's not on FOX cheerleading Trump & endless wars, he is attacking the very neighbors who gave him a chance. 2028 can't come soon enough."

Dnc Vice Chair Attacks Democratic Sen. John Fetterman: 'You're A Mess'

Conor Lamb, a former Pennsylvania congressman who ran against Fetterman in the 2022 primary for the party's nomination, called on Fetterman to resign.

"John, if there is a decent bone left in your body, just quit. It's an insult to decent people in our state for you to treat them and the office this way," Lamb wrote, referring to an instance where Fetterman blew off a meeting with paralyzed military veterans.

As reactions continue to pour in, Former Fetterman Staffers, the new group on X, told viewers that they would set a deadline for some of its upcoming revelations.

"Set your calendar for September 14th — the day the Senate is back in session — for our first drop. (Let's be honest, maybe the 15th: he'll skip Monday's votes)," the group said.

Despite raising questions and rage toward Fetterman, some observers condemned the staffers for what they called a lack of loyalty.

"So disloyal. He gave you jobs and opportunities and advanced your careers, and you publicly turn on him and set up an X account to attack him?" Marc Thiessen, a political pundit and former White House speechwriter for the Bush administration, wrote on X.

"Honorable thing, if you disagree, is to resign quietly and work for someone else you prefer. You are pathetic."

Mark Morgan, political director for the Republican Governors Association, echoed Thiessen's thinking, blasting the group for its anonymity.

"Staff rule #1: it's not about you Staff rule #2: Your boss had the courage to put their name on a ballot. If you've chosen to become a click-seeking bottom feeder, at least have the courage to put your own name on it," Morgan said.

Embattled Rep Tony Gonzales Announces Plans To Resign Amid Sexual Misconduct Allegations

"I'm disgusted by anonymous leakers, actually," Harmeet Dhillon, Trump's assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division at the U.S. Department of Justice, added.

Fetterman's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.
