title: Wisconsin businesses say they 'dodged a bullet,' rejecting high taxes as democratic socialist lost primary
description: WMC's Kurt Bauer says Wisconsin businesses "dodged a bullet" when Francesca Hong lost to David Crowley but warns concerns remain on taxes.
fullText:
Wisconsin businesses "dodged a bullet" when democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong lost the Democratic primary to a more moderate candidate, according to the CEO and president of Wisconsin Manufacturers & Commerce (WMC).

"My flip answer would be to open up a history book and learn how socialism has failed everywhere it's been tried, and it would fail here in Wisconsin as well. So, from that perspective, we've dodged a bullet in the state of Wisconsin," Kurt Bauer, WMC president and CEO, told Fox News Digital.

Bauer's comments came after state Rep. Hong fell short in her bid to capture the Democratic gubernatorial nomination in Wisconsin last month.

Democrat Establishment Strikes Back As Socialist Candidate Downed In Battleground Primary

The primary was closely watched as a high-stakes test of whether battleground Democrats favored the party's progressive wing or its establishment ahead of November's general election.

Hong, a state lawmaker from Madison and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), was defeated by Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who topped her by a razor-thin margin after polling had shown her with a significant lead.

Crowley will face off in November against Republican nominee Rep. Tom Tiffany, a House Freedom Caucus member backed by Donald Trump. The race is considered one of the GOP's top flip opportunities nationwide.

Wisconsin Democratic Voters Chalk Socialist Francesca Hong's Stunning Loss Up To Electability Concerns

Crowley was backed by retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, with both warning that nominating Hong could jeopardize Democratic control of the governor's mansion in November.

Hong's positions and efforts to backtrack from past statements, including previous calls to abolish the U.S. Senate and criticizing Thanksgiving, became issues during the campaign in Wisconsin, a perennial swing state.

"The person who won the primary said himself that he basically has the same policy that she has. So, he might be a little bit better on some of the issues, but he still represents, I think, a concern for the business community on taxes, on healthcare and some of the other major issues that they care about," Bauer told Fox News Digital.

WMC conducts a biannual survey of 200 business leaders to gauge how small businesses are affected by state policies.

According to the winter 2026 survey, business owners in Wisconsin expressed concern over the state's trajectory. WMC reported that 71% of businesses saw increases in property tax bills for their owned or leased commercial property over the past year, while just 1% saw a decrease.

According to WMC's report, nearly half of survey respondents said that President Donald Trump's tariffs had a negative impact on their business, while 12% reported a positive impact.

"Overall, Wisconsin employers seem to be lukewarm," Bauer concluded. "Although we see hints of optimism like increased hiring and a relatively good outlook for the U.S. economy, businesses are still frustrated with high healthcare costs and finding capable employees."

In response to Bauer's comments, Crowley's campaign sent Fox News Digital the following statement:

Meet The Democrat Who Narrowly Defeated Socialist Rival In Key Swing-state Battle Over The Party's Future

"Under David Crowley's leadership, major corporations have brought their business and thousands of jobs to Milwaukee County. As governor, he'll work with members of both parties to balance the budget and create good-paying, family-supporting jobs — just as he's done as county executive," a campaign spokesperson said.

"Meanwhile, Congressman Tiffany has supported every single one of Donald Trump's tariffs that are crushing Wisconsin's manufacturers and farmers and went years without paying his own taxes."

Primary Takeaways: Dems' Left-center Battle Intensifies As Schumer Takes Another Hit; Split Decision For Trump

Crowley has emphasized his track record supporting businesses. As Milwaukee County executive, Crowley secured millions in grants for local enterprises and helped negotiate bipartisan legislation to keep the Milwaukee Brewers in the city through state funding agreements.

His office credited the region's business-friendly climate with helping Milwaukee County's tourism industry generate $4.4 billion in total economic impact, contributing to Wisconsin's fourth consecutive record-breaking year for tourism. On the infrastructure front, Crowley implemented the Building Bridges program, which provides small businesses technical support and financial assistance through $10,000 grants.

State Of Play: Highly Watched Hong Race Remains Too Close To Call As Progressives Notch Key Primary Wins

Crowley's office announced that it secured federal funding, including an $8 million grant for a redeveloped terminal at Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport from the U.S. Department of Transportation. The move is expected to create hundreds of construction jobs.

He has received endorsements from several labor unions and trade associations, including the Wisconsin AFL-CIO, Plumbers Local 75 and the IBEW Wisconsin State Conference, which represents 15,000 electrical workers.

Bauer nevertheless praised Tiffany's record on business issues.

"We don't do actual endorsements, but we do get involved in the races. We have a 501(c)(4) for issue advocacy, so we will support pro-business candidates in the election. I'm not sure we will get involved directly in the governor's race, but we will certainly educate our members on what positions both the Democrat and Republican take on the issues that they care about," Bauer said.

"We have worked with Congressman Tom Tiffany from his days in the state legislature. We know him very well. We know what he stands for. He's been very pro-business. He's an ally of the business community. He wants investment into the state, and he understands that, in order to do so, you have to have the right business climate."

Fox News Digital spoke with Wisconsin business owners about their thoughts on the upcoming gubernatorial election and state economic policy.

Dane Leceski, owner of "Gents, Chaps, & Blokes" and a former political consultant, expressed a similar sentiment.

"I do believe that Wisconsin really dodged a bullet when it came to David Crowley winning over Francesca Hong," he said.

'Moderate' Dem Gubernatorial Candidate Embraced Dei Budget Tool, Green New Deal-style Policies

"David Crowley worked with Republicans and Democrats to balance budgets, deliver surpluses, expand affordable housing and pass property tax cuts in Milwaukee County," Crowley's campaign told Fox News Digital.

"Congressman Tom Tiffany didn't pay his personal income taxes for years, and his entire economic agenda is giving tax breaks to big tech billionaires by slashing healthcare funding. We can't trust Tom Tiffany to balance his own checkbook, let alone a multibillion-dollar budget."

Tiffany shot back at Crowley in a comment to Fox News Digital.

"My wife, Chris, and I owned and operated a seasonal dinner boat and excursion business in northern Wisconsin for nearly 20 years. Before we ever took home a dollar, we had employees counting on us, fuel to buy and a boat and equipment to maintain and improve. We paid all taxes owed in full and on time, and running that business is one of the reasons I got involved in public service," he said in a statement. "I experienced firsthand how regulations and government bureaucracy can make an already difficult job even harder.

"David Crowley has never run a small business. His record in Milwaukee County is higher property and sales taxes on families and small businesses. Taking that approach statewide would only make Wisconsin less competitive. We already ranked 40th in job creation from 2018 to 2025, and some rankings put us in the bottom 10 states to start a new business.

"As governor, I will lower taxes, cut unnecessary red tape and make Wisconsin a place where employers have every reason to invest and create jobs. Wisconsin has the people and the work ethic to lead the country. We just need a governor who will get government out of the way and let Wisconsin reach its full potential."

Fox News Digital also spoke with the Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA) after its political arm endorsed Tiffany for governor. The group stated its endorsements come "with no party affiliation" and stem from candidates' "voting records, public statements and responses to a candidate questionnaire."

"We like to think we're the political voice for the business owners, the builders, the racers, the manufacturers and enthusiasts that are empowering the automotive aftermarket industry, which has a $337 billion economic impact across the U.S.," Lauren Wilbor, a spokesperson for SEMA's SuperPAC, Driving Force Action, told Fox News Digital.

"We wanted to make sure that Tom Tiffany was that clear endorsement ahead of the primary because we felt like he was the clear choice to support Wisconsin's business economy and had real concern if Francesca Hong was elected."

Gregg McKarns, owner of Madison International Speedway, said he supports policies that protect local venues.

"While we have it good here in Wisconsin, we'd like to keep it that way. Just hearing about property tax increases — it's concerning because we're on 50 acres. We have a lot of land here, and we need a lot of land to run our business," McKarns told Fox News Digital.

Hong's campaign and Evers' office did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Fulham booed off after third defeat in a row
description: Fulham arebooed off by some supporters following the 3-2 Premier League defeat by Crystal Palace at Craven Cottage.
fullText:
Fulham were booed off by some supporters following the 3-2 Premier League defeat by Crystal Palace at Craven Cottage.

Having led twice in the first half, Alvaro Arbeloa's side fell to a third consecutive Premier League defeat since he replaced Marco Silva, who joined Benfica in the summer following five years in charge.

Josh King and summer signing Cesar Palacios scored in the first half, but a goal in each half from Tyrick Mitchell levelled the match twice before substitute Ben Chilwell scored the winner three minutes into his second Palace stint.

It leaves Fulham as one of only two sides to have lost their opening three Premier League games this season, alongside Coventry City.

It follows defeat at Sunderland and at home to Chelsea, which also finished 3-2.

Liverpool and Manchester United are next on Fulham's league fixture list before the extended September and October international break.

"We didn't deserve to lose this game," Arbeloa told BBC's Match of the Day.

"My players did everything - good attitude, they were brave, so many chances to score more goals.

"They [Palace] took their chances - in the end football is about that.

"We did many good things to win the game. It was similar against Chelsea but we lose.

"For the players it's a difficult situation, difficult moment, but I am very proud of them."

Chilwell scores on Palace return in win at Fulham

Fulham enjoyed a better expected goals (xG) of 3.13 than Palace (1.97), and also ran Chelsea close on the opening weekend.

But that does not stop the table reading three matches played, three defeats, zero points.

It led to booing from some Fulham fans, as well as chants questioning the team's performance.

Arbeloa will be no stranger to pressure. His playing career included more than 350 appearances for Real Madrid, Deportivo la Coruna, Liverpool and West Ham.

He also won 56 caps for Spain and was part of their side that won two European Championships and a World Cup between 2008 and 2012.

Arbeloa got the job following four months as Real's caretaker manager, taking charge of the final 28 matches of last season following Xabi Alonso's departure.

In that time he oversaw 18 wins, two draws and eight defeats.

As a former defender, the Spaniard will have wanted to avoid conceding three goals, especially in the manner they did.

"We were really unlucky in this goal [second Palace goal," Arbeloa said.

If Fulham can keep creating chances in the way they did against Palace, the victories should come. But the prospect of being on zero - or very few - points at the international break is a real one.

Arbeloa faces meetings with two of his former clubs next. A trip to Liverpool comes before a home Carabao Cup third-round tie with the Hammers and a league meeting with Manchester United.

Only six Premier League teams have started a season with five straight defeats. Of them, only two went on to avoid relegation.

Fulham made seven signings this summer. Of them, three followed Arbeloa in swapping the Bernabeu for Craven Cottage in Palacios, Gonzalo Garcia and deadline-day arrival Manuel Angel.

Palacios and Garcia have started all three league matches, while Northern Ireland midfielder Shea Charles was also handed a first league start against Palace following his £30m move from Southampton.

Palacios took his goal well, converting on the follow-up after Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson could only spill Jaydee Canvot's attempted clearance into his path.

Garcia, trusted to be Fulham's main source of goals this season, was unable to add to his tally against Palace, but did score on his debut against Chelsea and as a substitute in their EFL Cup second-round win over AFC Wimbledon three days later.

"Cesar Palacios and Gonzalo Garcia both had a great game. Cesar scored a goal, and for Gonzalo another great performance," Arbeloa added.

"Good effort from Gonzalo. That's the spirit I want from my players - the striker making a sprint to try and save a goal.

"With that spirit and character, if we play in this way the victories will come."

title: Pompey boss apologises as Cardiff's Bielik clashes with fan
description: Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho apologises to Cardiff City players after an incident involving home fans at Fratton Park during their Championship match.
fullText:
Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho has apologised to Cardiff City players after an incident involving home fans at Fratton Park.

In the 72nd minute of Portsmouth's 2-0 Championship win over the Bluebirds, Cardiff defender Krystian Bielik got into a physical altercation with a fan as he went to retrieve a ball.

Cardiff head coach Brian Barry-Murphy claimed afterwards that Bielik "got slapped in the face", while clips circulating on social media appeared to show the Poland international grabbing a young fan around his upper body.

Several Portsmouth supporters made gestures that indicated they believed the fan had been grabbed around the throat.

In the aftermath, another fan threw a ball at the head of Cardiff defender Perry Ng, which resulted in both fans being ejected from the stadium.

Speaking after the match, Pompey boss Mousinho said: "The referee said that, as Krystian went to get the ball, there was a little bit of a kerfuffle and one of the supporters struck him.

"It wasn't a good incident. I have just seen him there, and he was OK, but that's not the point, we can't be having that.

"We want to create a really difficult atmosphere at Fratton Park, we have done that successfully over the past few years.

"Sometimes it tips over, I understand that, I don't think it needs to tip over to that extent.

"We extend our apologies to the players, Cardiff and make sure we can try to cut it out."

Portsmouth secure first home victory against winless Cardiff

Championship: Boro beat QPR to go second; West Ham ease past Derby; Burnley bottom after Bristol City defeat

Cardiff boss Barry-Murphy described the incident as "not acceptable", but applauded the officials for their handling of the situation.

"Krystian went to get the ball back from the stands and got slapped in the face," said Barry-Murphy.

"I just wanted to make sure he was protected and make sure he was OK. He is.

"I thought the referee and his staff handled the incident impeccably.

"I think the players are always subjected to different things, it's not acceptable what happens.

"They don't expect that sort of treatment. My job is to protect the players but really my focus is on trying to make sure that we play well and win.

"So I'm sure the club and the FA (Football Association) will look at this and implement the correct process."

title: 'Not Football Manager' - De Zerbi says misfiring Spurs need time
description: Tottenham have failed to score in their opening three Premier League games and manager Roberto de Zerbi says it will take time to build his expensive squad into a team.
fullText:
It has been more than half a century since Tottenham have gone this long without a league goal to start the season.

A City Ground stalemate at Nottingham Forest at least gets Roberto de Zerbi's side their first point of the season but not to the extent they would want.

It followed defeats to Brentford and Newcastle which means Spurs have failed to score in their opening three league games for the first time since 1974-75.

Spurs did not play badly - they were the better side - but after their huge summer transfer outlay more is needed and expected.

De Zerbi preached patience and he is right - 10 senior arrivals means his team is still to find an identity.

And they did leave Forest with a point, something they have failed to do for almost three years.

Indeed, the video assistant referee's call to rule out Neco Williams' bundled second-half effort ensured it was not a third-straight Premier League defeat for Spurs.

Yet they have now failed to score in three successive Premier League games for the first time since November 2021, and improvement is needed at misfiring Spurs.

Last March's 3-0 win for Forest at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium provided the platform for the visitors' survival bid while leaving Spurs floundering until the final day.

Since then Spurs have spent over £300m on new players - contributing to the record £3.49bn Premier League outlay this summer.

Sandro Tonali, Jon Paul Van Hecke, Savio and Omar Marmoush were the new signings who started on Saturday, with De Zerbi remaining calm after another blank.

"We bought very, very good players but you can't just build the team with the names like in Football Manager," he told Sky Sports.

"We are disappointed for the result but for the performance very happy. Considering we started to work together last Thursday for the first time, for the first day.

"We have to improve in every part of football, organisation with and without the ball. Even today I thought we defended very well.

"We have to work because I think we played very well with the ball, we found the solution. I think we can be much better in the final third."

De Zerbi bemoaned Tottenham's decision-making with Marmoush a culprit, blazing over in the second half with Andy Robertson on an overlap and Mohammed Kudus waiting for a far-post tap in.

The former Brighton boss could see the positives but needs his men to discover their composure.

"I think we played well, in the last third we have to improve, we have to take better decisions, maybe keep calmer when we are close to doing something important.

"The chance when Marmoush shot, we had Robertson overlapping. If we take the right decision and if we play with Robertson on the second post there is Kudus to score.

"I am very happy with the spirit, with the organisation, their style of play is very clear, long ball and second ball, even the second ball we won many duels. They are good players.

"Taking a point in this stadium is not so easy. We are not happy because we didn't win but this is the right spirit and the right way to move on in this moment."

A draw was Tottenham's eighth in the league this year, their most across a calendar year since 2020, and they failed to have a shot on target in a top-flight match for the first time since April 2022 against Brentford under Antonio Conte.

Spurs have had 38 shots in the league this season with an expected goals of 3.3 and former midfielder Danny Murphy agreed with De Zerbi over what the visitors lacked.

"When Spurs did get in really good areas, they just rushed it and shot when they maybe should've passed," he told BBC Sport.

"They made the wrong choice on pullbacks or crosses when they're getting in wide areas, taking men on one too many times when they've already got the space.

"They were just missing that little bit of calmness and composure that you expect from top quality players.

"It takes time for some players [to find chemistry]. You could argue that Marmoush and Savio know each other anyway and bright footballers quickly learn each other's runs and movements.

"From a midfielder to a forward perspective, you're not always sure what they're going to do. Whereas if you played with someone for a while, it comes more naturally. So those relationships will build."

Mykhailo Mudryk arrived on deadline day, on an initial loan from Chelsea, looking to revive his career following his four-year ban for testing positive for banned substance meldonium in 2024, something he denied knowingly ingesting.

The Ukraine international came off the bench, his first Premier League appearance since being a second-half substitute in a 1-1 draw against Arsenal in November 2024.

"He needs time and he needs work, we have in that position Mathys Tel - big potential - but also Tel takes too many wrong decisions," added De Zerbi.

"Two big players with potential."

It was part of a second-half shake-up with Savio and Destiny Udogie being withdrawn after an hour in a planned double substitution on medical advice.

De Zerbi added: "Before the game the plan for Savio and Udogie was around 60 minutes. I'm not happy but football is like this, Savio not in the best physical condition to play 90 mins, he's a crucial player for us.

"Destiny is another crucial player. Kudus and Robertson played well but to start one game like today is not so easy to come inside from the bench and adapt immediately.

"I'm not happy when we have the plan but it's not my business, the management of players after injuries."

title: South Africa finish strongly to take 2-1 series lead against All Blacks
description: South Africa eventually overpower a spirited New Zealand as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 series lead.
fullText:
Greatest Rivalry Series - third Test

Tries: Arendse, penalty try, Kriel, Marx Cons: Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Mngomezulu

Tries: Savea 2, Jordan, Taukei'aho Cons: Love, McKenzie

South Africa eventually overpowered a spirited New Zealand, who could only outrun their hosts' set-piece power for so long, as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 lead in a high-quality 'Greatest Rivalry' series.

The two sides traded two tries each in a tight first half, with New Zealand's composure and ambition with ball in hand stretching South Africa's onrushing defence.

The All Blacks sniffed a famous victory when Will Jordan chased after his own kick ahead and crossed for a 17-12 lead in the 55th minute.

But, shortly after, Jesse Kriel barged through Leroy Carter to cross at the other end and, reprieved, South Africa took full advantage.

Malcolm Marx plunged over at the back of juggernaut maul and a Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty gave South Africa a cushion that Samisoni Taukei'aho's final-play try could dent, but not fully deflate.

The two teams will meet in a fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore next weekend, with New Zealand, who won the opening match, looking to snatch a draw in the series.

With Springbok captain Siya Kolisi calling on his team to honour those who died in nearby Soweto during the fight against apartheid, and national pride stung by New Zealand coach Dave Rennie's criticism of their scrum technique, Soccer City was braced for a fast start by the hosts.

New Zealand's smarts initially defused the fire and fury inside the cauldron, however.

After a brave Peter Lakai turnover had halted South Africa momentum, Will Jordan streaked clear to switch play to the other 22.

South Africa fly-half Feinberg-Mngomezulu was shown yellow for knocking down Ardie Savea's offload and, from the resulting penalty, the All Blacks rolled round the back of a short-range line-out, clearing room for Savea to sweep through some under-staffed fringe defence and score.

With Cheslin Kolbe, with a perfect goal-kicking record so far in the series, having departed with a head knock, South Africa had taken a dent to their confidence, as well as the scoreboard.

New Zealand had ducked and dived to minimise the effect of South Africa's set-piece supremacy.

Fast strikes from hooker Asafo Aumua had got the ball away from a fast-retreating scrum, while trick plays and the addition of Lakai as a jumping option kept South Africa from competing successfully at the line-out.

South Africa built momentum regardless though and All Black discipline frayed as Damian de Allende shrugged off Carter and fed Kurt-Lee Arendse to score in the 21st minute after a string of penalty offences from the away side.

New Zealand pulled back 12-5 ahead soon after with the agility and speed of second rows Sam Darry and Tupou Vaa'i buying territory and Savea on hand to scoop up and scoot over following Arendse's tackle on Carter out wide.

It is impossible to keep the South Africa's coshing scrum power out of the game, however.

Rennie had accused South Africa's front row of 'walking around' their opposite numbers in their second Test win in Cape Town last weekend. Marx, Wilco Louw and Ox Nche duly took route one, ploughing through the All Blacks front row to force a penalty try and ensure parity at half-time.

While another Test awaits in the United States, the sense of an unofficial series being on the line was tangible.

New Zealand have won on South African soil only once before, when the Incomparables of 1996 returned with a 2-1 victory.

Fly-half Ruben Love missed a long-range shot at goal after the interval with the stakes suffocatingly high.

Jordan's try, from Carter's pop off the floor, briefly opened up scoreboard space on 55 minutes, but South Africa edged ahead for the first time two minutes later as Kriel shrugged off a soft tackle and scampered in.

The hosts took a 19-17 advantage into the final quarter and, with the All Blacks lacking Savea's leadership after their captain was forced off with a shoulder injury in the first half, the Boks landed a knockout blow in familiar fashion.

Scrum pressure forced New Zealand replacement Fletcher Newell to his knees, the Springboks punted the resulting penalty into the 22m and a monster maul rumbled infield and forward with Marx crashing over.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu added the extras for a 26-17 lead and slotted a 70th-minute penalty to push the lead out to 12 points.

The 85,976-strong crowd went through their celebratory songbook, dusting off their Cranberries-inspired ode to head coach Rassie Erasmus.

Taukei'aho's try was too little, too late to change the tune of the contest, but the rest of the rugby world will take heart from how hard his side have pushed the Springboks in all three of their meetings.

South Africa: Kolbe; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi, PS du Toit, Wiese

Replacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, Libbok

New Zealand: McKenzie; Jordan, Tupaea, J Barrett, Carter; Love, Roigard; Bower, Aumua, Lomax, Vaa'I, Darry, Lakai, Jacobson, Savea

Replacements: Taukei'aho, Numia, Newell, Holland, Sititi, Preston, Lienert-Brown, Moorby

title: Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash
description:
Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech
Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.
The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas.

fullText:
Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech

Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.

The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas.

Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Data and polling from the Washington Post show that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year. Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroying the cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan.

“In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.”

Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor, blocked state agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, is promising to introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna is cosponsoring a bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras.

Municipal leaders of all political stripes are dropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes they replace the license plate readers with another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing.

Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue.

“Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?”

Americans have been showing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations.

While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another.

“Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University.

Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond.

“The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”

fullText:
Workers who blame algorithms for lowering their earnings are getting help from academics to find out how the system works

Gig economy workers are urging delivery platforms to open up the “black box” of computer-driven algorithms that determine the jobs they are offered and how much they are paid, blaming increased use of AI for lowering wages.

A group of food delivery riders in Edinburgh say their rates of pay have fallen and their working conditions have deteriorated at the same time as Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat, the three dominant gig economy platforms in the UK and Ireland, have increased their use of automation.

“I am making half the money I was making four years ago, for the same amount of hours. It makes no sense,” said David, a food delivery rider in Edinburgh for the past seven years who did not want to share his surname.

On a weekday afternoon in the Scottish capital, David and other food delivery riders are sharing their experiences of worsening pay and conditions before they go their separate ways to carry food and groceries to customers’ doorsteps during the dinnertime rush.

Standing next to their bikes and insulated food delivery bags in central Edinburgh’s Bristo Square, many have cycled the city streets for several years and tracked a gradual decline in the amount they are paid, even though they continue to deliver similar numbers of orders.

The group has come together through the Workers’ Observatory, a charity founded by gig economy workers alongside academics at St Andrews and Edinburgh universities. Its aim is to help riders research the parts of their working experience that are mostly concealed by the companies that operate delivery platforms, to help them to challenge their working conditions.

David’s experience is echoed by Xabier Villares, who has been riding for eight years and is now the observatory’s lead organiser. “There has been a dramatic change in the last three years,” he said. “I used to work four or five days a week, especially evenings and some lunchtimes, and was able to pay my rent and bills and make a decent living with that. But that’s not an option any more.”

The observatory, which has just gained research funding for the next decade, has previously carried out experiments to monitor the variable levels of pay offered to different workers by algorithms, a system known as “dynamic pricing” that purports to match real-time supply and demand.

Trades unions are campaigning to ban the practice, saying it leaves workers uncertain about their earnings.

The introduction of a dynamic pricing algorithm in 2023 resulted in Uber drivers earning “substantially less” an hour, according to research from the University of Oxford and New York’s Columbia business school.

This week drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countries launched a landmark class action against the ride-hailing app claiming they live in “constant fear” of the “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs.

The legal case lodged in Amsterdam, which could run into billions of dollars, alleges the AI-powered system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings based on what each driver is willing to take. Uber denies adjusting trip prices based on an individual driver’s behaviour and has put discrepancies down to other features of its system such as GPS.

Cailean Gallagher, director of the observatory and a lecturer at St Andrews university business school, said “there is so much infrastructure of knowledge and data that’s concealed” by the platforms, leaving gig economy riders “working in the dark”.

He added: “What we are trying to do with the observatory is to get on the ground floor in terms of understanding how the whole apparatus works.”

In one Workers’ Observatory test, a group of riders in Dunfermline, Fife, logged on to a delivery platform at the same time, with some rejecting job offers below a certain rate. This boosted the rate for some workers in the short term, while others were penalised – with one deactivated from the platform shortly afterwards, although it was unclear why – in a way that Gallagher says “seemed very arbitrary”. The major delivery platforms insist riders are not deactivated for rejecting job offers.

Dylan* has notched up more than five years riding for Deliveroo in Scotland. Since mid-2023, he has kept meticulous records tracking his monthly income, number of orders delivered and what the average pay per order is.

The number of orders Dylan delivers each hour has remained constant between 3.6 and 3.8 for the past three years. However, his records highlight how the average fee paid for each order has steadily declined over that period, from £3.67 in 2023, to £3.63 in 2024, £3.51 in 2025 and to £3.42 in the first half of 2026.

“I like to keep a close eye on everything, normally just to make paying my taxes easier,” he said. “I started noticing a couple of years ago there was actually a big drop-off in my earnings. If you are doing the same amount of work, that equates to getting paid quite a lot less for the same work.”

Dylan blames the algorithm for constantly undercutting rates, along with the introduction of what Deliveroo calls “stacked orders”, where riders can accept two or three orders from restaurants located close to each other, but not receive the level of fees they would get for delivering these separately. “Some of the offers they give you view you as a clown,” he said.

Rider Graeme Frances believes the delivery platforms “rely on [the work] being opaque”. He said: “You don’t know what is in the black box of how they work out what to pay to whom.”

Deliveroo has named its algorithm Frank and has previously described it as “super smart” and able to decide “which rider to offer which order”. The company, which was taken over by its US rival DoorDash in 2025, said Frank was “made up of machine-learning technology, which predicts the timings of every order”, allowing food to be delivered “in the most efficient and reliable way”.

Frances also blames increased use of AI by the platforms for more log-on difficulties. After ending up with a black eye following an accident outside work in August 2025, the facial recognition technology did not allow him to log-on to the Deliveroo app, preventing him from working. He was unable to get help from human support staff.

Deliveroo acknowledged Frances failed the facial recognition checks multiple times, stopping him from working, which it said was due to a blurry picture.

Frances says he requested a manual review of his facial recognition check and was not aware he had passed this until the next time he logged in, leading him to believe he could not work until his injury had healed. Deliveroo says Frances would have been able to work after the manual review.

Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat all say their riders earn more than the national living wage while they are on an order, but this does not include time waiting for job offers.

A Deliveroo spokesperson said: “Riders are guaranteed to earn a minimum hourly fee while on an order, which … rose by 3.8% this year – an above inflation increase.

“The vast majority of riders are satisfied working with us, and we continue to partner with the GMB Union to raise the bar on security and wellbeing standards. Information on our algorithm and fees are set out on our rider website.

“We have a dedicated team in place to support riders, and any significant decision over a rider account is not automated, but reviewed by our team.”

An Uber spokesperson said: “Our matching tools follow a process that balances a number of different factors, such as time and distance, to provide the best possible experience for everyone using the app.”

A Just Eat spokesperson said: “As a delivery platform we use technology, overseen by a human team, to match deliveries with available couriers.”

Milei finds unity in pushback against Falkland Islands oil project
description: Milei finds unity in pushback against Falkland Islands oil project
fullText:
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 5 (Reuters) - Argentines have broadly backed President Javier Milei’s forceful push against oil drilling near the Falkland Islands, underscoring the enduring resonance of Argentina’s sovereignty claim over the British-controlled archipelago.

In a televised address on Thursday, Milei said he would submit a bill to Congress to toughen sanctions against companies drilling and participating in "other activities on the islands that impact our natural resources."

Milei previously favored diplomacy over confrontation on the Falklands. Argentina has claimed sovereignty over the Falkland Islands for nearly two centuries and lost a war with Britain over them in 1982. Britain said on Friday its position was "unwavering."

Because Argentina does not administer the islands, it cannot directly block drilling there.

In Buenos Aires, Mariana Hamicha, a 49-year-old accountant, said Milei’s tougher stance signaled Argentina was standing up for its interests.

"I think taking a firm stand, especially regarding the exploitation by foreign companies and the extraction of oil, can be a way of drawing a line in the sand," Hamicha said.

Milei also proposed creating a national security council to coordinate across aerospace and maritime security policy, and pledged more funding for a naval base in the southernmost province of Tierra del Fuego, a strategic gateway to the Falkland Islands and Antarctica. The government has not provided further details on the bill.

“What Milei understood is, this is the moment to act,” said Juan Battaleme, a former secretary of international affairs for defense under Milei.

Milei’s speech came days after President Donald Trump suggested the U.S. could reconsider its neutral stance, citing frustration with Britain’s limited support for U.S.-led military operations in the Middle East.

The Sea Lion ​oilfield north of the Falkland Islands is operated by majority owner Navitas Petroleum, with Rockhopper Exploration owning 35%. The two owners have strong ties to Israeli investors.

The companies said on Friday they had ​valid petroleum licenses and did not think Milei’s comments would affect the project. Shares of both companies fell sharply on Friday.

Candela Mascetti, a researcher at the Escuela Superior de Guerra in Buenos Aires, said Milei’s remarks marked a notable shift for a president often criticized for not giving enough attention to the Falklands issue.

“I don’t think having a naval base implies a call to arms, but it’s a posture that we hadn’t seen from Milei’s government in such a strong way,” Mascetti said.

Falklands War veterans and the left-wing opposition have criticized Milei for praising former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, whose government defeated Argentina in the war over the islands, as one of the world’s "greatest leaders." He also said Argentina hoped islanders would "one day decide to vote for us," a comment critics said echoed Britain’s emphasis on the residents’ right to self-determination.

Milei, expected to run for reelection in 2027, has a low approval rating of 36.8%, according to an August poll by Zuban Cordoba and Associates.

"Given Milei’s poll numbers — and Trump’s hints that he is reconsidering the U.S. position on the dispute — it makes sense that Milei is adopting a harder line," said Benjamin Gedan, director of the U.S.-based Stimson Center’s Latin America program.

Even some of his political opponents welcomed Thursday’s announcement, while criticizing Milei for not taking aggressive action earlier.

Juan Grabois, a prominent leftist leader, said on X: “Milei’s 180-degree turn is welcome; he went from being a colonized fool to reclaiming Argentina’s historical stance.”

Guillermo ​Carmona, who oversaw Argentina’s policy regarding its claim to the Falklands under the previous center-left government, said Milei’s measures were a positive step but insufficient given Argentina’s close diplomatic ties to Israel.

"Milei has to pressure the Israeli government," he said.

Israeli officials did not respond to a request for comment on Milei’s proposed sanctions.

Ex-NFL agent: Giants RB Cam Skattebo's margin for error is shrinking
description: A former NFL agent believes the representatives of New York Giants RB Cam Skattebo must step in and save him from himself.
fullText:
The New York Giants are entering the 2026 NFL season with a running back room that has a little bit of everything. They have experience, depth, toughness, and versatility.

That is, if everyone can stay healthy and focused.

Which brings us to the case of second-year back Cam Skattebo, who became a folk hero last year in just eight games. Skattebo, a fourth-round pick out of Arizona State, suffered a fractured ankle midway through the season, but not before capturing the hearts and imagination of Giants fans.

His smashmouth style and straightforward approach to the game and life in general may not support a long NFL career. People are taking notice, most notably Giants' head coach John Harbaugh.

"Skatt's great. He does bring a lot of energy," Harbaugh said last week after Skattebo started a skirmish with defensive players at practice.

"But he did get a 15-yard penalty at the end of practice. Did you notice that? That's not infectious. Well, it is infectious, actually. Infectious in a bad way, right? Like an infectious disease type of thing (laughs). We don't want that. So, we want it to be directed in a positive way."

That's the issue. Skattebo has one speed. Full throttle. Joel Corry, a former NFL agent, believes Skattebo needs to be reined in. If the Giants won't do it, maybe his agent, or reps, should.

When situations like these arise, an agent should provide counsel to their client. It's an agent's job to tell a client what he needs to hear, not what he wants to hear. That isn't always done. Some agents are reluctant to be candid for fear of being fired and instead become enablers.

The initial backflip created an opportunity to warn Skattebo about the risk he was taking, considering he hadn't completely recovered from a serious injury. Had there been a major setback that jeopardized or ended Skattebo's 2026 season, which fortunately didn't occur with either backflip, he would have landed on the Reserve/Non-Football Injury list (NFI).

Corry is referring to the backflip Skattebo performed earlier this year at Fanatics Fest, where he didn't stick the landing. For a player who had not shown he could play football yet with his reconstructed ankle, this opened a lot of eyes. Not in a good way, either.

The Giants are aware they can't corral Skattebo completely. His persona is what it is. He's reckless in every direction he goes, so they had to go out and get themselves some insurance.

In free agency this year, they signed Pro Bowl fullback Patrick Ricard to lead the way out of the backfield. Ricard will take on the tacklers that Skattebo was taking head-on. It should free up some running room and spare Skattebo some wear and tear.

Then the Giants signed 232-pound Najee Harris to take early snaps and soften up the defense. That was Skattebo's job. Was.

Skattebo is talking about having a 2,000-yard season. That will happen maybe if he averages 20 yards per carry. His workload will be managed to the point where he might get anywhere from eight to 12 carries per game, max.

With Harris in tow and the team still very much aware that Tyrone Tracy Jr. is their only back with any measurable speed, Skattebo is in a committee situation with the Giants. Let's not leave out Devin Singletary, who is on the roster to provide a quick change-up a half-dozen times a game.

Skattebo may not want to pace himself and change, so the Giants could be quietly doing it for him.

This article originally appeared on Giants Wire: Ex-NFL agent: Giants RB Cam Skattebo's margin for error is shrinking

fullText:

Katie Taylor enters the ring one last time on September 5 against Flora Pili. Not only will she look to end her career once again as an undisputed champion, but Taylor will finally compete at the legendary Croke Park.

Taylor (25-1) has beaten some boxing's best. She's a former undisputed lightweight champion. After suffering her first loss against Chantelle Cameron, Taylor beat Cameron to hold all the gold at super lightweight. "The Bray Bomber" is coming off a historic trilogy against Amanda Serrano.

It's been an emotional week for the 2012 Olympic gold medalist. As she heads off into the sunset, Taylor, for the final time, looks to entertain the 80,000 fans that came to see her last dance.

"It's going to be an amazing night for Irish sport, Irish boxing and women's sport in general," Taylor said. "… I'm so, so grateful for the support. I'm blown away by it to be quite honest. I want to put on a performance worthy of everyone's support over the years."

A former French national champion, Pili (12-0) has held European gold at super lightweight. Pili last fought in December, beating Jelena Janicijevic to earn her first shot at world gold.

title: Newcastle 2-2 Bournemouth: What Rose said
description: Since the start of last season, Bournemouth have dropped the joint-most points from winning positions in the Premier League (29 – level with Newcastle), and the outright most by any team in away matches (18).  Bournemouth are the first team in Premier League history to score the opening goal in their first three games of a season and fail to win any of them (D2 L1).
fullText:
Bournemouth manager Marco Rose, speaking to BBC Match of the Day: "It is what it is. We started really well. We played a top first half. Our pressing was impressive. The opponents had no solutions. We scored two goals and had more chances. Then we conceded in pretty much with the first chance for the opponents.

"In the second half, we dropped a bit in everything. Even we didn't get real trouble in our box but we conceded again a late goal. This is disappointing but I'm really happy with the confidence the lads came here today to take the three points. At the end, we have to work on the things we need to improve. And that's what we will do in the coming days.

"We knew that it's going to be intense against Newcastle. We defended Anthony Elanga really well. We did all that but in the end, if you are 2-0 up and you have the chance to score a third goal, you should do it or you have to defend your goal better than we did."

On conceding late again: "I try my best. Even the lads. It's not with intention to do it. Sometimes you have phases where things like these happen. We should go for our first win the Premier League to calm down this kind of talks.

"Regarding the points, I am not happy. We just have two now. It's about results in this level. But performance wise, I see a lot of good things."

Since the start of last season, Bournemouth have dropped the joint-most points from winning positions in the Premier League (29 – level with Newcastle), and the outright most by any team in away matches (18).

Bournemouth are the first team in Premier League history to score the opening goal in their first three games of a season and fail to win any of them (D2 L1).

title: New method predicts where massive earthquakes will strike
description: UC Riverside scientists have developed a way to identify where Earth's biggest earthquakes are most likely to occur, offering a powerful new tool for improving disaster preparation in some of the most dangerous seismic regions.
fullText:
edited by 
 Andrew Zinin

UC Riverside scientists have developed a way to identify where Earth's biggest earthquakes are most likely to occur, offering a powerful new tool for improving disaster preparation in some of the most dangerous seismic regions.

Rather than predicting the timing of an earthquake, the method identifies where stress has been building along major faults, allowing scientists to determine where a rupture is likely to take place.

In a recent test detailed in a Geophysical Research Letters paper, the researchers found that their model highlighted the exact section of the Kamchatka subduction zone in eastern Russia where a massive earthquake later occurred.

The study was led by UCR geophysicists Gareth Funning and Axel Periollat, who study how Earth's surface slowly deforms as tectonic plates lock together before rupturing.

"Earthquakes capture headlines when they happen, but for years beforehand the fault is quietly accumulating strain," Funning said. "This strain can be measured."

The team's approach focuses on subduction zones, where one tectonic plate slides beneath another. These regions generate Earth's largest earthquakes, including those exceeding magnitude 8.5, and often produce devastating tsunamis.

Using GPS measurements of subtle ground movement, the researchers developed an algorithm that identifies portions of faults that are locked and storing energy. These locked regions, known as asperities, act like patches of friction that resist motion until enough stress builds to trigger a major earthquake.

The researchers had identified one such locked region beneath Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula before a large earthquake struck there. While the timing of the event was beyond the scope of their method, the rupture occurred exactly where their model indicated strain had accumulated.

"We had an idea where the strain was accumulating based on a relatively limited data set," Periollat said. "Seeing it work so well confirmed that this approach has real potential."

The findings also revealed that earthquakes occurring in the same region can behave differently. Although Kamchatka experienced giant earthquakes in both 1952 and 2025, the more recent event generated a much smaller tsunami, suggesting the shallowest portion of the fault slipped less than during the earlier rupture.

The researchers emphasize that their method cannot predict tsunami size or earthquake timing. However, narrowing where the greatest hazards exist could improve long-term planning and preparedness.

The team is now applying their approach to other major subduction zones in Japan, Mexico, New Zealand and the Pacific Northwest. Each presents additional complexities, such as events that release energy gradually rather than in sudden earthquakes.

They are also exploring whether similar techniques can improve understanding of California faults.

"In the Bay Area, the Hayward Fault has both creeping and locked sections, much like subduction zones," Funning said. "We're investigating whether we can identify the parts most likely to generate future earthquakes."

Applying the method more broadly will require better observations. While GPS stations on land provide valuable information, scientists have far fewer measurements offshore, where many of the world's most dangerous faults lie beneath the ocean.

Researchers in Japan have begun using acoustic instruments placed on the seafloor to measure slow deformation over many years, and similar efforts are being proposed elsewhere, including Chile and the Pacific Northwest. A recently launched satellite could eventually provide additional measurements in regions that currently lack GPS coverage.

The work also highlights major gaps in global earthquake monitoring, particularly in parts of the Pacific where limited data make it difficult to assess tsunami hazards.

The researchers stress that improved forecasting of earthquake locations should complement, not replace, public preparedness.

"Your peace of mind shouldn't come from believing we can forecast the exact earthquake," Funning said. "Especially where we live in Southern California, it's not a matter of if, but when. There is no substitute for preparation."

The team believes their algorithm could eventually help scientists evaluate seismic hazards at many of the world's most active plate boundaries, provided sufficient data become available.

"We can identify where large earthquakes are likely to occur, even if we can't predict exactly when," Periollat said. "With better observations and continued monitoring, we can learn much more about Earth's most dangerous faults."
