title: How London City proved they can live up to the hype
description: There was an expectation on London City Lionesses to live up to the hype and deliver in the Women's Super League's season opener - and they did.
fullText:
There was an expectation on London City Lionesses to live up to the hype and deliver in the Women's Super League's season opener - and they did.

Eder Maestre's side showed they are not just a starting XI of superstars but a team who may gel quicker than many expected.

They came away from Hayes Lane, in front of a full crowd of 5,402 home fans, with an impressive 2-1 victory over Manchester United.

The scoreline could have been worse for United as London City dominated the first half and showed flashes of individual brilliance, amid a clear structure and intent.

Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas made her debut and was the glue in midfield while others stole the limelight.

US billionaire owner Michele Kang was also present, donning a new match shirt with her name on the back and posing for photos with fans before kick-off.

"It was really fun to win today," said Delphine Cascarino, one of many international stars in the London City squad.

"I think we have a chance to do something this season. We are trying to build something huge and achieve big things and I think we have a chance."

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

The tone was set in the first minute by London City, immediately showing their intent with a strike from Alanna Kennedy in the first minute that won a corner.

They allowed United no time to settle, pressing from the front and taking advantage of the visitors' hesitancy in possession.

A flick from Putellas here and there, tenacity from Kennedy and quick feet from Grace Geyoro were all frequently on show.

But it was the fluidity of London City's link-up play that caught the eye - a group of superstars looking like a good team in the first game of the season.

Surely it pleased manager Maestre?

"Yeah, I think we were really strong, mostly in the first half," said Maestre.

"We are facing Manchester United. You can't imagine you will be dominant for the whole game because they have a lot of good players.

"The team showed how capable we are and what we were trying to create so I'm very proud."

London City were a bit of an unknown entity in pre-season given the arrival of several big-name players.

Ex-United and England goalkeeper Mary Earps started on the bench alongside fellow new arrival Nicole Anyomi but Spain's Mapi Leon and forward Rosa Kafaji started.

Danielle van de Donk, who spent most of last season injured, starred and scored, while Kennedy's header brought the opener when it deflected off Julia Zigiotti.

Putting the pieces together is the challenge with which Maestre has been tasked but Friday night was a fine start.

"It's one of the most challenging situations for coaches when you have many talented players but you are trying to align everyone on the same page and achieve something big," said Maestre.

"We need very good positional game and that flexibility to feel strong in a match. That is why I'm really happy with the performance.

"To have all the players on the same page and establish that relationship is really good."

In contrast, opponents Manchester United - one of those London City hope to overtake this season - clearly need more time to adapt to new manager Eva Olid's ways.

When she addressed the media for the first time on Thursday, the Spaniard promised brave, attacking football and a desire to dominate possession.

But what transpired in a painful opening 45 minutes for United supporters was a team short on confidence and lacking threat, failing to produce a shot of any kind.

The second half saw improvement but it came too late.

Indeed, United did not have a shot on target until the ninth minute of second-half stoppage time, substitute Simi Awujo's goal giving the scoreline a friendlier look.

"I always say it's a process. In three weeks, I don't think we can believe we are a team that will dominate the ball and attack," said ex-Hearts boss Olid, who was appointed on 5 August.

"Of course, I think it's more something mental. In the first half, I didn't feel like the players were believing. At half time I said: 'Listen, this is not us.'

"In the first half, we were forcing things, the basics in possession were wrong and we were giving them the ball to attack. That is not what we want to be.

"In the second half, we were building through the middle, playing in the pockets and moving through the lines. That is us. That felt like my team in the second half."

Olid said it was her job to help her players believe they can be better and was defiant when asked if United could compete with the quality displayed by London City.

She said the difference between the two teams on the day was down to confidence.

"If we play as we did in the second half, I don't think the gap is that big," she added.

"I think the structure was wrong in attack - when the structure isn't right, the players are lost. We fixed that but mentally, the players were not believing.

"London City pressed well and took our mistakes to create chances. They did very well in the first half but in the second half, I felt we were in the match."

title: Opinion - India-France ties should not replace relations with Washington
description: France and India have increasingly strengthened their technological, economic and especially military relations.
fullText:
On its face, France and India do not have much in common. France is a NATO ally; India has remained outside any alliance system. France had numerous colonies around the world and maintains relations with many of them since they achieved independence. India was not one of those countries — it was the jewel in the British crown.

Yet both states have a common self-perception as independent poles in a multipolar world.

Despite its membership of NATO, France's long-standing refusal to join NATO's nuclear planning group reflects both its determination to maintain the independence of its nuclear deterrent and policy of what president Emmanuel Macron calls "strategic autonomy." And he is extending a French nuclear umbrella to other European states.

India, like France, is a nuclear power. It too has long pursued an independent national security policy. New Delhi did have close military and economic relations with the Soviet Union and still is a major purchaser of Russian oil. Nevertheless, the former leader of the non-aligned group of nations has no formal alliances and does not seek any.

Although France and India have maintained good relations since India achieved independence in 1947, their ties reached a turning point in 1998. That was when India conducted five nuclear tests and Washington issued sanctions against India. France did not. Indeed, France upgraded its strategic relationship with India that year.

Since the turn of the century, France and India have increasingly strengthened their technological, economic and especially military relations. Apart from counterpart visits by leading military and civilian officials, as well as naval visits, the two countries have conducted bilateral naval exercises since 2001; air force exercises since 2003; army exercises since 2011. India has also participated in the French-led multinational Orion exercises.

India has been a market for French armaments. These include India's 2016 purchase of 36 Rafale aircraft; its 2025 acquisition of 26 Rafale-M fighters for its aircraft carriers; and a 2026 additional purchase of 114 Rafale fighters. In addition, in 2005 India purchased designs for six French Scorpene submarines that it built domestically. India has recently ordered three more submarines from France.

Last year the French Directorate General of Armaments and the Indian DefenseResearch and Development Organization signed a broad-based agreement to deepen their  collaboration. This included, among other areas, "aeronautical platforms, unmanned vehicles, advanced materials… cyber security, artificial intelligence ... advanced sensors ... [and] underwater technologies." The agreement built upon a long-term strategic plan that the two countries formulated in 2023, termed Horizon 2047.

Finally, after an exchange of visits by French president Emmanuel Macron and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and on the recommendation of India's parliamentary standing committee on defense, New Delhi and Paris began discussions last month on Indian participation in the French Future Combat Air System that will develop a sixth generation fighter.

In contrast with their deepening mutual relations, both countries not only have had a historically uneasy relationship with Washington, but they also have a common apprehension  about the direction that American national security and economic policies have taken. France, as a member of the European Union, constantly lives under the shadow of new American tariffs imposed on EU products, or those that it produces on its own.

For example, in June, President Trump threatened to hit the French wine industry with a 100 percent tariff if it did not drop its digital services tax on American technology companies. Whether he will make good on that threat is unclear, but French apprehension should come as no surprise.

India also faces the threat of American tariffs. In early September the Senate passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act that imposes a 100 percent tariff on the five leading importers of Russian oil. India is one of them. The legislation is stalled in the House, but it could pass during the lame-duck period after the November elections.

Both countries also have recent grievances regarding American policies. France lost its sale of Barracuda submarines to Australia because of the AUKUS agreement, which provided for a British-American solution to Canberra's requirement for new submarines. India, ever suspicious of Pakistan, has resented Washington's reliance upon Islamabad as a go-between in Washington's on-again off-again negotiations with Iran.

Like other states, notably in the Middle East, Paris and New Delhi are jointly hedging their bets against what they perceive might be future American policies. That is not an outcome that will benefit the U.S. France's policy of extending its deterrent umbrella should complement the American deterrent, not replace it.

As an increasingly powerful player in Asia, India should work alongside, rather than apart from, Washington's efforts to deter an increasingly aggressive China. There is much to be said for the blossoming French-Indian partnership, but it should not come about because of a loss of faith in American reliability.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

title: Rabbinic group accuses Jewish entertainers of 'whitewashing antisemitism' in Mark Ruffalo defense
description: The Coalition for Jewish Values accused over 170 Jewish entertainers of whitewashing antisemitism by defending Mark Ruffalo's merger criticism.
fullText:
FIRST ON FOX — A rabbinic group is calling out some Jewish entertainers for "whitewashing antisemitism" by supporting actor Mark Ruffalo after his harsh opposition to the proposed Warner Bros. Discovery-Paramount merger.

More than 170 Jewish entertainers and artists signed a letter Tuesday "proudly" voicing support for Ruffalo after he was accused of antisemitism when criticizing the proposed $111 billion merger.

Coalition for Jewish Values, which represents over 2,500 traditional, Orthodox rabbis in American public policy, said it typically does not respond when a Hollywood figure says something it finds hateful about Jews or Israel. But the group believes Ruffalo's comments forced a group of Jewish Hollywood figures that have "little knowledge of Jewish history or the nature of antisemitism" to "deny obvious bigotry."

More Than 180 Jewish Entertainers Rally Behind Actor Mark Ruffalo In Protest Letter

"Ruffalo did not merely criticize a business deal. In an August 22 Instagram post tying the Paramount-Skydance/Warner Bros. merger to Oracle's work with Israel, Ruffalo claimed that the Ellison family — who are Jewish — were 'powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world,' and framed a corporate transaction as built on 'genocide' and 'apartheid.' That is not policy criticism, but mischaracterization of civil rights for Jews and Arabs as racism, and the rescue of Jewish hostages as murder," the Coalition for Jewish Values said in a statement.

"Nonetheless, more than 170 Jewish entertainment figures rushed to sign a letter dismissing the antisemitism charge as an 'outrageous smear campaign.' To be certain, they are entitled to their ignorant and misguided views," the statement continued. "They are not, however, entitled to be taken seriously when they engage in whitewashing antisemitism, or suggest that those with sufficient discernment to recognize the oldest of anti-Jewish tropes should deny the obvious."

The group said that "America set itself apart from much of the world precisely by declaring hatred of Jews unwelcome, regardless of who dressed it up as righteousness," and feels "Ruffalo would do well to remember that he owes much of his career to the Founding Fathers who made America so hospitable, and the Jews who fled persecution in Europe to build new homes for their children in a friendlier land."

John Cusack Stands In 'Solidarity' With Mark Ruffalo Amid Paramount's Antisemitism Allegation

"It is some of those children, working in New York in the early 20th century, who created Marvel Comics and invented The Incredible Hulk," the group said.

Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, told Fox News Digital that Ruffalo's remarks were "embarrassing" and that Ruffalo presented a "mythical inversion" of the situation in the Middle East.

Ruffalo was accused of invoking "antisemitic tropes" by Paramount after the Marvel star shared a video from August of Safra Catz, an Oracle executive vice chair and Paramount board member, discussing technology Oracle used to assist Israel after the Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attack.

He linked Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, to financing behind the proposed acquisition and suggested the merger would be used to push "oppression."

"These 'really profoundly scary technologies' will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you," Ruffalo said. "Look how she revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle."

Antisemitic Violence Reaches Deadliest Level Since 1994, New Global Report Finds

title: Trump says Iran conflict, which has killed 18 US service members and injured hundreds more, is ‘small potatoes’
description: President Donald Trump on Friday labeled the Iran war “small potatoes,” the latest attempt to minimize a six-month conflict that caused a spike in gas prices and led to the deaths of 18 American servi...
fullText:
President Donald Trump on Friday labeled the Iran war "small potatoes," the latest attempt to minimize a six-month conflict that caused a spike in gas prices and led to the deaths of 18 American service-members.

"A lot of people don't call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing," he said in the Oval Office.

A day earlier, Vice President JD Vance said the conflict shouldn't be termed a "war" since major combat operations ended months ago.

Trump similarly cast the conflict as periodic and low-grade, despite routine rounds of back-and-forth strikes.

"I would say that it's intermittent. You know, we do intermittent strikes," Trump said, adding: "There's a lot of truth that we're not fighting right now. There's no fighting."

This week the US said it had targeted nearly 60 military targets around the Strait of Hormuz — including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites — while simultaneously escorting ships through the waterway.

The administration had signaled it was moving past a military strategy, focusing instead on choking off Iran financially by applying sanctions on its trading partners. So far, however, the US has stopped short of punishing China, Tehran's biggest economic lifeline.

Trump, who plans to host Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit this month, downplayed the assistance Beijing was providing.

"They are not really involved. Very little involvement by China. China could have plenty of involvement," he said.

He also extolled potential new routes and pipelines that could bypass the Strait of Hormuz, including an overland alternative through Syria.

"They're going to end up with a horrible strait that's not really necessary any more," he said.

Trump also raised the prospect of a new operation soon to take out a suspected Iranian nuclear site south of Tehran.

"We may hit Pickaxe very soon," he said, referring to the underground facility where Iran is believed to have moved some of its stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

But he still insisted the conflict was not a war.

"It's a military conflict, but it's very intermittent. I could see somebody not calling it a war," he said.

He continued: "I don't think it matters what you call it. What matters is the fact that we have had tremendous success."

This story has been updated with additional details.
